h-rider-haggard: Henry Rider Haggard was born at Bradenham, Norfolk, the eighth of ten children of William Meybohm Rider Haggard, a barrister, and Ella Doveton, an author and poet. Unlike his elder brothers he attended Ipswich Grammar School, because his father could no longer afford expensive private schooling and perhaps doubted that he would amount to much. After he failed his army entrance examination he was sent to a London crammer to prepare for the Foreign Office examination, which he never sat. In London he met people interested in the study of psychic phenomena.

In 1875 his father sent him to South Africa as an unpaid assistant to the secretary to Sir Henry Bulwer, Lieutenant-Governor of Natal. In 1876 he joined the staff of Sir Theophilus Shepstone, Special Commissioner for the Transvaal, and in April 1877 he was in Pretoria for the announcement of the British annexation of the Transvaal. He raised the Union Flag and read much of the proclamation after the official chosen lost his voice. In 1878 he became Registrar of the High Court in the Transvaal. He married Marianna Louisa Margitson in 1880 and returned to England in 1882, settling at Ditchingham, Norfolk. He was called to the bar in 1884.

His legal practice was desultory, and after a book on the political situation in South Africa and a few unsuccessful novels he completed King Solomon's Mines, published in September. He accepted a 10 per cent royalty rather than £100 for the copyright. Allan Quatermain, She and its sequel Ayesha followed, with Nada the Lily, a tale of the Zulus, and the Viking romance Eric Brighteyes. Haggard also worked for agricultural reform and sat on commissions on land use. He stood unsuccessfully as a Conservative for East Norfolk in 1895, losing by 197 votes, and was knighted in 1912.

Haggard died on 14 May 1925 in Marylebone, London, aged 68, and his ashes were buried at St Mary's Church, Ditchingham. His novels carry many stereotypes of colonialism, yet they treat African characters with unusual sympathy; Africans often play heroic roles, such as the Zulu warrior Umslopogaas. Critics have also condemned his depiction of non-Europeans, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o names him among the canonical authors he calls geniuses of racism. Carl Jung read Ayesha as a manifestation of the anima, and the first chapter of People of the Mist is credited with inspiring the Royal Air Force motto Per ardua ad astra.
ha-long-bay: Hạ Long Bay lies in northeastern Vietnam and is administered by the city of Quảng Ninh. The name Hạ Long means descending dragon. The bay covers about 1,553 km2 and holds 1,969 islets, most of them limestone, with a core area of 334 km2 that has 775 islets. Several of the islands are hollow, with large caves; Hang Dau Go is the largest grotto in the area.

Surveys show that people lived in the area tens of thousands of years ago. The Soi Nhụ culture, a people of the coast who caught fish and shellfish and gathered fruits and roots, was followed by the Cái Bèo culture, whose inhabitants had reached the level of exploiting the sea, and then by the Hạ Long culture. Before the 19th century the name Hạ Long Bay had not been recorded in the country's old books, and the bay was called other names such as An Bang, Lục Thủy and Vân Đồn. In the late 19th century the name appeared on a French maritime map. French tourists who visited the cave of Hang Dau Go at that time named it the Grotte des Merveilles.

The channels near the bay were the setting for naval battles against Vietnam's neighbours. On three occasions the Vietnamese army stopped Chinese invaders from landing among the channels of the Bạch Đằng River. In 1288 General Trần Hưng Đạo stopped Mongol ships from sailing up that river by setting steel-tipped wooden stakes that were covered at high tide, sinking the fleet of Kublai Khan.

On 5 June 1948 the Halong Bay Agreements were signed by High Commissioner Emile Bollaert and President Nguyễn Văn Xuân, and the new national flag of the Provisional Central Government of Vietnam was raised for the first time. During the Vietnam War many of the channels between the islands were heavily mined by the United States Navy, and some mines still threaten shipping routes.

In 1994 the core zone of the bay was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site for its aesthetic value, and in 2000 the World Heritage Committee also recognised its geological and geomorphological value. Tourism has led to the clearing of mangroves and seagrass beds, and the province of Quảng Ninh has banned coal and stone extraction in the heritage area and moved fishing households from floating villages to the mainland.
haakon-vii: Prince Carl was born on 3 August 1872 at Charlottenlund Palace north of Copenhagen, the second son of Crown Prince Frederik of Denmark, the future Frederick VIII, and Louise of Sweden. Through his mother he was a grandson of King Charles XV of Sweden and Norway, which linked him to both the Danish and Swedish royal houses. As a younger son he was third in line to the Danish throne, with little prospect of inheriting it. He was educated at the Royal Danish Naval Academy and served in the Royal Danish Navy. On 22 July 1896 he married his first cousin Princess Maud of Wales; their only child, the future Olav V, was born in 1903.

The union between Sweden and Norway, in existence since 1814, was dissolved unilaterally by the Storting on 7 June 1905, and the Norwegian people confirmed this in a referendum on 13 August. Sweden recognized it on 23 September in the Treaty of Karlstad. Carl was offered the Norwegian crown, accepted after a referendum on the monarchy and was elected by the Storting, taking the Old Norse name Haakon. He was the first independent Norwegian monarch since Olav IV in 1387. He arrived in Kristiania on 25 November 1905 and was crowned in Trondheim on 22 June 1906.

Although the Constitution vested him with considerable executive powers, parliamentary rule had existed in Norway since 1884, so nearly all decisions were made by the Council of State in his name. He confined himself to a representative role, a practice continued by his son and grandson, and his long rule gave him considerable moral authority as a symbol of unity.

Germany invaded Norway in the early hours of 9 April 1940. Oscarsborg Fortress sank the heavy cruiser Blücher, which delayed the occupation of Oslo and allowed the royal family, the cabinet and most Storting members to leave by special train. German bombers attacked Nybergsund on 11 April, but the king and his ministers escaped into the woods. Haakon rejected German demands to legitimise the Quisling regime, vowing to abdicate rather than do so, and he refused to abdicate in exile.

In Britain his wartime speeches were broadcast to Norway by the BBC, which established him as a national symbol of resistance. He returned to Norway in June 1945 and limited himself to constitutional duties. He died at the Royal Palace in Oslo on 21 September 1957 and was succeeded by Olav V.
haapsalu: Haapsalu lies on the west coast of Estonia and is the administrative centre of Lääne County. Its name derives from the Estonian words haab, aspen, and salu, used in an archaic sense for a forested island. Until the first half of the 20th century it was called Hapsal in Swedish and German. The town has six neighbourhoods: Holmi, Kesklinn, Männiku, Paralepa, Randsalu and Vanalinn.

The first written record of Haapsalu dates from 1279, when the town was chartered and became the capital of the Bishopric of Ösel-Wiek, which it remained for the following three centuries. The episcopal castle survives, and its church is the largest single-nave church in Estonia. From the 13th century Haapsalu and the surrounding area were the centre of the Estonian Swedes, until almost all ethnic Swedes were evacuated from Estonia in 1944, before the Soviet invasion.

In 1825 a military doctor, Carl Abraham Hunnius, founded the first mud cure resort there, because the sea mud was claimed to have a curative effect. News of the curative mud spread quickly among wealthy customers in Saint Petersburg and elsewhere in the Russian Empire, and the Romanov family frequented the mud spas. In 1867 Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky wrote a suite of three piano pieces during his stay, titled Souvenir de Hapsal.

Haapsalu is a seaside resort town with a population of 9,375. For almost 200 years it has been a summer destination for people seeking medical treatment with the sea mud, and three mud cure establishments operate there. In the 19th century the town became known for the Haapsalu shawls, a delicate craft made by local women. It hosts summer festivals, among them the August Blues Festival and the White Lady Days. The Haapsalu Horror and Fantasy Film Festival has been held there annually since 2005.
haarlem: Haarlem lies on the river Spaarne, about 20 km west of Amsterdam and near the coastal dunes. It stands on a thin strip of land above sea level known as the strandwal, which connects Leiden to Alkmaar, where people struggled against the North Sea to the west and the waters of the IJ and the Haarlem Lake to the east. The city became wealthy from the tolls it collected from ships and travellers on this busy north–south route. For centuries it was the centre of the tulip bulb-growing district.

The oldest mention of Haarlem dates from the 10th century, and a Christian parish church has stood there since the 9th. The first city walls were built in 1270. Beer brewing was important from the 15th century, when there were 100 breweries in the city, and clean water from the dunes also served the bleaching trade.

After the Geuzen conquered Brielle, Haarlem began to support them, and King Philip II of Spain sent an army north under Don Fadrique. It besieged the city on 11 December 1572. The defences were commanded by the governor Wigbolt Ripperda, and a widow, Kenau Simonsdochter Hasselaer, helped defend the city with some three hundred other women. A great fire on the night of 22 to 23 October 1576 began in a brewery near the weighhouse. The Spanish left in 1577.

To restore the economy and attract workers, the council promoted the arts and showed tolerance for diversity of belief. Haarlem declined in the 18th century as trade gravitated to Amsterdam. On 19 January 1795 a bloodless revolution removed the city's administrators the night William V fled the country, and the Batavian Republic was proclaimed.

Haarlem is the capital of the province of North Holland. Teylers Museum, on the Spaarne, is the oldest museum in the Netherlands, and the Frans Hals Museum houses Dutch master paintings. The city is known for its hofjes, almshouses built around courtyards, of which 19 survive.
haber-process: During the 19th century the demand for nitrates and ammonia, for use as nitrogen fertilisers and as industrial feedstocks, grew rapidly. The main sources were mined niter deposits and guano from tropical islands, and at the beginning of the 20th century these reserves were thought insufficient for future demand. Atmospheric nitrogen makes up about 78 percent of the air but is exceptionally stable and does not readily react with other chemicals. The cyanamide process, its chief competitor at first, used large amounts of electrical power and was more labour-intensive.

Fritz Haber and his assistant Robert Le Rossignol developed the high-pressure devices and catalysts needed to demonstrate the process in the laboratory. In the summer of 1909 they made ammonia from the air, drop by drop, at about 125 millilitres an hour. The German company BASF bought the process and set Carl Bosch to scale up Haber's tabletop machine. Haber was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1918 and Bosch in 1931, for overcoming the chemical and engineering problems of large-scale, continuous-flow, high-pressure technology.

Nitrogen and hydrogen gas react on the surface of a solid catalyst, usually iron, to form ammonia. The two nitrogen atoms in each molecule are held by a very strong triple bond, which must be broken before they can react. This is the slowest step and controls the speed of the whole process. The reaction needs high pressure and high temperature, and the synthesis loop works at 300 to 500 °C. Only about 15 percent of the gases turn into ammonia on each pass, so the ammonia is cooled and removed as a liquid and the unused gases are recycled. Most of the hydrogen comes from natural gas. The first catalysts Haber used were based on osmium and uranium.

The first industrial plant opened in 1913 at Oppau. During the First World War Germany used the process to make nitric acid for explosives, which it could no longer import because of the Allied blockade. Most of the ammonia is used for nitrogen fertiliser, either directly or as ammonium nitrate and urea. Vaclav Smil writes that with average crop yields at the 1900 level the harvest of the year 2000 would have needed nearly four times more land. In 2018 the process produced about 230 million tonnes of ammonia, using 1 to 2 percent of the world's energy and contributing to the buildup of reactive nitrogen in the biosphere.
habib-bourguiba: Habib Bourguiba was born in Monastir, the youngest of eight children. His father had spent nineteen years campaigning in the army and later became a city councilman, which allowed him to pay for his son's modern education. Bourguiba attended Sadiki College and the Lycée Carnot in Tunis, took his baccalaureate in 1924 and graduated from the University of Paris and Sciences Po in 1927. He returned to Tunis in August 1927 to practise law, and in the early 1930s joined the Destour party.

After the riots of 9 April 1938 he was sent to Marseille, where he was held during the Second World War. Following his release in 1945 he went to Cairo to seek the support of the Arab League, and he returned to Tunisia in 1949. In 1950 he travelled to Paris and set out the nationalists' demands in seven points. When talks failed, unrest began in 1952, and he was imprisoned on La Galite Island for two years before being moved to France. There he negotiated with Prime Minister Pierre Mendès France, who recognised Tunisia's internal autonomy on 31 July 1954.

Bourguiba came back to Tunis on 1 June 1955 and then faced Salah Ben Youssef, who rejected his gradual policy and called for the independence of the whole Maghreb. The dispute set Bourguibists against Youssefists and ended in Bourguiba's favour at the Sfax Congress of 1955. Independence was proclaimed on 20 March 1956. Bourguiba became prime minister under the bey and proclaimed the Republic on 25 July 1957.

On 8 February 1958 the French army bombed the border village of Sakiet Sidi Youssef, killing 72 people, and Bourguiba responded by banning French warships from Tunisian waters. His government's reforms covered female emancipation, public education, family planning, state healthcare and the ending of religious endowments known as waqf, and the Code of Personal Status was the main one. He also built a presidential system. The Neo Destour was declared the only legal party in 1963, and in 1975 he proclaimed himself president for life.

The 1980s brought Bourguiba's declining health, a struggle over his succession and a political and social crisis. On 7 November 1987 his prime minister, Zine El Abidine Ben Ali, removed him from power. He was kept in a house in Monastir until he died there on 6 April 2000, and he was buried in a mausoleum he had built earlier. His supporters called his pragmatic doctrine Bourguibism. He is remembered for leading Tunisia to independence and for founding its republic.
hadrians-wall: Hadrian's Wall was probably planned before the emperor's visit to Britain in 122. Hadrian ended the expansionist policy of his predecessor Trajan and concentrated on defending the existing borders. Britain had no natural boundary, such as the Euphrates, Rhine or Danube, to divide the Roman province from the peoples of the north.

Building began in 122, and most of the work took about six years. It was done by soldiers of three legions, the Legio II Augusta, Legio VI Victrix and Legio XX Valeria Victrix, some 15,000 men in all, together with some members of the Roman fleet. The wall ran for 80 Roman miles, equivalent to 73 modern miles, from Segedunum at Wallsend on the Tyne to the shore of the Solway Firth near Bowness-on-Solway. Its planned thickness of 10 feet was soon reduced to about 8 feet. West of Milecastle 49 it was first built of turf and later replaced in stone.

The wall was built with an alternating series of forts, each housing 600 men, and milecastles manned by between 12 and 20 men, with a turret every third of a mile. After construction almost 10,000 soldiers were probably stationed along it, drawn not from the legions that built it but from regiments of auxiliary infantry and cavalry raised in the provinces. Troops in the forts had the primary duty of defence, while those in the milecastles and turrets were responsible for frontier control.

Roman coins and pottery generally did not cross the wall, which seems to have been an effective barrier to trade. After Hadrian died in 138 his successor Antoninus Pius began the turf Antonine Wall about 160 km to the north, leaving Hadrian's Wall occupied in a support role. Marcus Aurelius abandoned the Antonine Wall and reoccupied Hadrian's Wall in 164.

Almost all the standing masonry was removed in early modern times for local roads and farmhouses, and long sections were used in the 18th century to build General Wade's military road. The antiquarian John Clayton, town clerk of Newcastle in the 1830s, saved much of what remains by buying land along the wall. Hadrian's Wall became a World Heritage Site in 1987. It lies wholly in England and has never formed the Anglo-Scottish border.
hafez: Khajeh Shams-od-Din Mohammad Hafez Shirazi was born in Shiraz and identified as a Sufi Muslim. Few details of his life are known, and accounts of his early years rely on traditional anecdotes; the early tazkiras, or biographical sketches, that mention him are generally considered unreliable. He is said to have memorized the Quran at an early age, and the title Hafez, which he later used as his pen name, was given to him for this.

He was supported by the patronage of several successive local regimes, among them Shah Abu Ishaq, who came to power while Hafez was in his teens, and the strict Mubariz ud-Din Muhammad. His work flourished most under the 27-year rule of Jalal ud-Din Shah Shuja. Hafez also exchanged letters and poetry with Ghiyasuddin Azam Shah, the Sultan of Bengal, who invited him to Sonargaon; he could not go.

Hafez wrote chiefly lyric poetry in the form of the ghazal. His Divan, probably compiled after his death, deals with the beloved, faith, wine and taverns, and the exposure of hypocrisy. Whether the poems are to be read literally, mystically or both has been disputed. William Jones saw a conventional lyricist like Petrarch, Henry Wilberforce Clarke a poet of ecstatic mysticism like Rumi, and Ralph Waldo Emerson rejected the Sufi reading of wine. The argument arises because early Persian poetic vocabulary was taken over by mystics, so that no 14th-century lyric could avoid a mystical flavour; Hafez embraced the fusion.

According to an account by Jami, Hafez died in 1390. Twenty years later a tomb was raised for him in the Musalla Gardens in Shiraz; the present mausoleum was designed by André Godard in the late 1930s. There is no definitive version of the Divan: editions run from 573 to 994 poems. Hafez was acclaimed across the Islamic world in his lifetime, and William Jones first translated him into English in 1771. In Iran families open the Divan at random on Nowruz and Yalda Night and read the poem as a sign of what will come.
hafez-al-assad: Hafez al-Assad was born on 6 October 1930 in Qardaha, a town in northwest Syria, into a poor Alawite peasant family of the Kalbiyya tribe. He was the ninth son of his father Ali al-Assad, who had eleven children. He became the first in his family to attend high school, in Sunni-dominated Latakia, where he faced anti-Alawite bias, and he joined the Ba'ath Party in 1946. He wanted to study medicine, but his father could not pay, so in 1950 he entered the Homs Military Academy and then the flying school in Aleppo. He graduated in 1955 as a lieutenant in the Syrian Air Force.

Assad, Salah Jadid, Muhammad Umran and others established the Ba'ath Military Committee, and he was a key participant in the 1963 coup that brought the party to power. He was appointed commander of the Syrian Arab Air Force. After a second coup in February 1966 he became Minister of Defense under Jadid, who gave him de facto control of the army. Four years later Assad initiated a third coup, ousting the quasi-Marxist Jadid, and became prime minister in 1970. A referendum approved him as president on 12 March 1971.

In power he dropped Jadid's policy of exporting socialist revolution and allied Syria with the Soviet Union while keeping ties with some Western European and Gulf states. Syria fought Israel in the 1973 Yom Kippur War, and in 1976 it invaded Lebanon with 30,000 troops. Syria remained a one-party system, with decision-making placed under the president's control. From 1973 to 1976 an Arabization campaign known as the Arab Belt deported around 140,000 Kurds from 332 villages in the north-east. His regime crushed an Islamist uprising led by the Syrian Muslim Brotherhood through crackdowns that culminated in the Hama massacre, in which two thirds of the city was destroyed.

Assad's eldest son Bassel, his chosen heir, died in a car crash in 1994, and he turned to his younger son Bashar, then a medical student abroad. He demoted officials who opposed the succession. Assad died in office in June 2000 and Bashar succeeded him. Hafez al-Assad exerted considerable influence on the politics of the region; the New York Times wrote that no lasting peace could hold without him, but none could be negotiated with him either.
hagia-sophia: Justinian's building was the third church on the site. The first, known as the Magna Ecclesia, or Great Church, because of its size, was consecrated on 15 February 360 under the emperor Constantius II. A second church, ordered by Theodosius II, was inaugurated on 10 October 415. It was destroyed, and on 23 February 532, only a few weeks later, Justinian began a third and entirely different basilica, larger and more majestic than its predecessors. He appointed two architects to design it, the mathematician Anthemius of Tralles and the geometer and engineer Isidore of Miletus.

The dome is carried on four spherical triangular pendentives, making the building one of the first large-scale uses of that element. It was the largest pendentive dome in the world until St Peter's Basilica, and its height is much lower than that of any other dome of such a diameter. After the vault first collapsed, the dome was rebuilt in 558. The church stayed the largest in the world for more than five hundred years, until the abbey church at Cluny was completed in the 12th century. The horseshoe-shaped upper gallery was reserved for the empress and her court. The Imperial Gate was originally used only by the emperor.

Under Justinian the interior had abstract designs on marble slabs and mosaics on the vaults, with a few figurative decorations. Figurative mosaics added later were destroyed during the iconoclastic controversy of 726–843, and the surviving mosaics are post-iconoclastic. The minarets are Ottoman additions, and the two western ones, by Selim II and designed by Mimar Sinan, are 60 metres high. Sinan also directed the building of buttresses, and 24 were added in all.

For nearly a thousand years Hagia Sophia was the religious centre of the Eastern Orthodox Church. In 1054 the envoy of Pope Leo IX, Humbert of Silva Candida, delivered the excommunication of Patriarch Michael I Cerularius there, an act considered the start of the East–West Schism. In 1204, during the Fourth Crusade, it became a Catholic cathedral under the Latin Empire, and it was restored to the Orthodox Church in 1261. Enrico Dandolo, the doge of Venice who led the Crusade, was buried in the church.

After Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Empire on 29 May 1453, Mehmed II performed the Friday prayer there and ordered its conversion to a mosque. It was the principal mosque of Istanbul until the Sultan Ahmed Mosque was built in 1616. Mustafa Kemal Atatürk made it a museum in 1935, and in 2020 it was reclassified as a mosque. Its style became the model for Eastern Orthodox church architecture and was emulated by Ottoman mosques, including the Şehzade Mosque and the Süleymaniye Mosque.
haifa: Haifa lies on the Israeli Mediterranean coastal plain, at the mouth of the Kishon River and on the northern slopes of Mount Carmel around Haifa Bay. The city is split over three tiers: the lowest holds commerce, industry and the port, the middle level the older residential districts, and the upper level modern neighbourhoods. It is about 90 km north of Tel Aviv. The origin of its name is unclear; proposals include the high priest Caiaphas, a Hebrew root meaning to cover or shield, and the Hebrew words for 'beautiful shore'.

The earliest known settlement nearby was Tell Abu Hawam, a port and fishing village founded in the Late Bronze Age, in the fourteenth century BCE. Haifa is first mentioned in Talmudic literature about the third century CE, as a Jewish fishing village whose fishermen caught murex snails for purple dye. After the Arab conquest of the Levant it was overshadowed by the port of Akka.

Shortly after the First Crusade the crusaders took Haifa after a fierce battle with its Jewish inhabitants and Fatimid garrison, and it became a small fortified stronghold in the Principality of Galilee. Saladin's army captured it in July 1187 after the Battle of Hattin, and the crusaders under Richard the Lionheart retook it in 1191. In the 1760s the old settlement was moved 2.5 km east as a fortified town, today the Old City.

British forces captured Haifa in September 1918. Its population was 98 percent Arab in 1872, and Jewish immigration from 1881 changed the balance, so that by 1945 it was 55 percent Jewish and 45 percent Arab. During and after the Battle of Haifa in the 1948 war most of the Arab population fled or was expelled, and the Old City was later demolished.

Haifa is the third-largest city in Israel, with 297,082 inhabitants in 2024. The Baháʼí World Centre, a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a destination for Baháʼí pilgrimage, stands there. The city has a major seaport, the Technion and the University of Haifa, and the Carmelit underground railway. About ten percent of the population is Arab.
haiku: Haiku grew out of the opening verse of renga, a long collaborative form of linked poetry, and of its later derivative renku. That opening verse was called hokku, and its position made it the most important, since it set the tone for the whole composition. By the time of Matsuo Bashō (1644–1694) the hokku had begun to appear as an independent poem, and it was also used in haibun, a combination of prose and hokku, and in haiga, a combination of painting with hokku. Bashō raised haikai from a playful game of wit to serious poetry. Yosa Buson (1716–1784) was also a master of haiga, and Kobayashi Issa (1763–1827) made the genre accessible to wider audiences. Masaoka Shiki (1867–1902) gave the form its present name.

A traditional Japanese haiku has three phrases of five, seven and five on, the sound units called morae. A word such as haibun counts as four on in Japanese though two syllables in English, so a poem of 17 on may hold only 15 syllables. A kireji, or cutting word, usually ends one of the phrases and acts like a caesura or a sonnet's volta. A kigo, a word implying the season, is drawn from a list called a saijiki. These rules were not absolute: Bashō himself wrote a haiku of 18 on in a 6-7-5 pattern, and some verses lack a kireji. Free-form haiku, advocated by Ogiwara Seisensui and his disciples, give up the 17-on pattern.

Several women learned haiku from Bashō or his disciples in the early 18th century, among them Chiyo-ni. Hendrik Doeff, a Dutch commissioner at Dejima, wrote haiku in the early 19th century, and Paul-Louis Couchoud introduced haiku in France around 1906. They influenced the Imagists, notably Ezra Pound's poem of 1913, In a Station of the Metro. R. H. Blyth's four volumes of 1949–52 introduced haiku to the English-speaking world after the war. The carving of haiku on stone, as monuments called kuhi, has been a custom for many centuries.
hainan: Hainan consists of Hainan Island and more than 200 smaller islands in the South China Sea. Its name literally means South of the Sea, after its position south of the Qiongzhou Strait, a channel 20 kilometres wide that separates it from the Leizhou Peninsula of Guangdong. The province has a land area of 33,920 square kilometres, almost all of it the island, which is slightly smaller than Taiwan. Wuzhi Mountain, at 1,840 metres, is the highest peak. The climate is mostly tropical, and the island holds over 1,500 square kilometres of tropical forest. Earlier names for the island include Zhuya, Qiongya and Qiongzhou.

Hainan Island was recorded by Chinese officials in 110 BCE, when the Western Han dynasty established a military garrison there after the arrival of General Lu Bode. Over many centuries imperial authorities exiled people condemned as criminals or political dissidents to Hainan and northern Vietnam, where banished people were put to harsh labour in the tropical climate. The Hlai, a Kra-Dai-speaking people, are native to the island.

After 1912 Hainan was organised as the Qiongya Circuit within Guangdong, and in 1920 Sun Yat-sen proposed a Qiongya Special District. The Hainan Special Administrative District was formally established in 1949. On 1 May 1950, under the People's Republic of China, it became an Administrative Region Office, a branch of the Guangdong provincial government. On 13 April 1988 the National People's Congress decided to establish Hainan Province, and Deng Xiaoping's reform and opening up programme made it a special economic zone.

The capital is Haikou on the northern coast, and Sanya on the southern coast is a well-known tourist destination. Han Chinese make up 82% of the population and the Hlai 15%. Most people speak Hainanese, a variety of Min Chinese, and most practise Chinese folk religion and Chinese Buddhism.
haiphong: Haiphong lies at the mouth of the Cấm River in the north-eastern coastal area of Vietnam. Its territory covers 3,194.72 square kilometres and includes the islands of Bạch Long Vĩ and Cát Bà and the Long Châu islands in the Gulf of Tonkin. The climate is humid subtropical, with hot, humid summers and warm, dry winters, with most rain between April and October.

Haiphong was the home of Lê Chân, one of the women generals who served the Trưng Sisters in their rising against Chinese rule in 40 CE. The rising lasted until 43 CE. Lê Chân is said to have established the Hải tần Phòng thủ, the Defense of the Coast, in the war against the Han general Ma Yuan.

Under French rule Haiphong ranked as a first-level city equal to Saigon and Hanoi, and in the last years of the nineteenth century the French proposed to make it the economic capital of Indochina. After the defeat of Japan in World War II, Vietnamese nationalists pressed for independence against the French return. French forces landed at Haiphong and met resistance in which three French soldiers died. In retaliation French ships, among them the cruiser Suffren, shelled the city and set it ablaze, an event that precipitated the First Indochina War. French infantry under Jean-Étienne Valluy then entered, fighting house to house with armour and aircraft in support.

In the Vietnam War the city was bombed by United States Navy and Air Force aircraft. Admiral Thomas H. Moorer ordered the mining of the harbour on 8 May 1972, effectively sealing the port. The mining caused no casualties, and the city's buildings were largely unaffected, as the United States had set a prohibited zone around the city. After the war Haiphong recovered its role as an industrial centre.

Haiphong is a major port, the Port of Haiphong standing on the Cấm River, and a centre of shipbuilding, steel and plastic pipes, textiles, cement and food processing. It is the first city in Vietnam and in mainland Southeast Asia to have been electrified. Route 5 leads west to Hanoi and Route 10 south towards Nam Định. A railway built by the French links the city with Hanoi and with Lao Cai on the Chinese border.
haiti: Haiti forms the western three-eighths of Hispaniola, the second-largest island of the Greater Antilles, and shares a border of 360 km with the Dominican Republic. It is the most mountainous country in the Caribbean, with plains covering only 22% of its territory, and the highest point is Pic la Selle at 2,680 m. The name comes from the Taino language and means land of high mountains. It was the native name for the whole island, and Jean-Jacques Dessalines restored it as the official name of independent Saint-Domingue, in tribute to the Amerindian predecessors.

Indigenous peoples have lived on Hispaniola for about 6,000 years. Arawakan-speaking ancestors of the Taino arrived during the 1st millennium BCE, and at the time of European contact the island was divided among five caciquedoms led by chiefs. Christopher Columbus landed on 6 December 1492 and claimed the island for the Crown of Castile. The 39 men he left behind founded La Navidad but were later killed by the Taino.

European diseases caused epidemics among the native people, the first recorded smallpox epidemic in the Americas breaking out on Hispaniola in 1507, and the encomienda system, which forced natives to work in gold mines and plantations, reduced their numbers further. Spain held the island until 1697, when the western part was ceded to France as Saint-Domingue, a plantation colony worked by enslaved Africans.

The Haitian Revolution of 1791 to 1804 made Haiti the first sovereign state in the Caribbean and the first country in the Americas to abolish slavery officially. The independent state began as an empire, later split into two and reunited in 1820, and a second empire under Faustin Soulouque ended with the return of the republic in 1859. The 19th century brought instability, international isolation and a crippling debt to France. United States forces occupied Haiti from 1915 to 1934, and the Duvalier family ruled as dictators from 1957 to 1986.

Haiti is a republic with Port-au-Prince as its capital and largest city, and about 11 million people, the most in the Caribbean. Its culture blends French and African customs with Spanish and Indigenous influences. The Citadelle Laferrière, built between 1805 and 1820, and the Sans-Souci Palace were inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1982.
haitian-creole: Haitian Creole took shape in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, where French colonists lived beside enslaved Africans who spoke various Niger-Congo languages. Its vocabulary comes largely from the French of the eighteenth century, but its grammar follows West African patterns, particularly those of Fongbe and Igbo. Words from Wolof, Fon, Kongo, Spanish, Taino and others also entered it. Often the French definite article stayed attached to the noun: la lune, the moon, became lalin.

In Saint-Domingue people of all classes spoke a Creole French, with lower and higher registers according to education and class, and it served as a lingua franca through the West Indies. The first written text in the French-lexicon creole is said to be a poem, Lisette quitté la plaine, composed in 1757 by Duvivier de la Mahautière, a white Creole planter.

Haitian Creole is not mutually intelligible with standard French. Its grammar is analytical: verbs are not conjugated, tense, mood and aspect are shown by markers placed before the verb, and there is no grammatical gender.  The definite article follows the noun. Many words that look like French have shifted in sense: frekan, from fréquent, means insolent or rude.

Spelling is phonemic and highly regular. The official system, set out by the Institut Pédagogique National, uses 32 symbols and keeps only the grave accent, on è and ò. It built on an orthography devised in 1940 by the Irish Methodist missionaries H. Ormonde McConnell and Primrose McConnell and revised with Frank Laubach. The three main dialects are the Northern, Central and Southern, centred on Cap-Haïtien, Port-au-Prince and Les Cayes.

Its place in schools and public life has been contested since at least the nineteenth century. Some Haitians see French as bound up with colonialism, while Francophones have dismissed Creole as the French of the uneducated. Until the late twentieth century Haitian presidents addressed their fellow citizens only in standard French, and until the twenty-first century elementary teaching was in French, a second language for most pupils. Even so, literary works in Creole existed by the end of the nineteenth century, among them Oswald Durand's Choucoune and Georges Sylvain's Cric? Crac!

The 1987 constitution named Creole and French the official languages and recognised Creole as the only language all Haitians share. It is spoken by more than 13 million people, including large communities in the United States, Canada, Cuba, the Dominican Republic and the Bahamas, and it is the most widely spoken creole language in the world.
haitian-revolution: In 1789 Saint-Domingue produced 60 percent of the world's coffee and 40 percent of the sugar imported by France and Britain, and its largest sugar plantations and concentrations of enslaved people lay in the north. Enslaved people were kept in check by whipping and worse punishments. The Code Noir of 1685, issued to regulate the treatment of the enslaved, was openly and consistently broken. The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen of 26 August 1789 was ambiguous about slaves and colonial citizens. After the revolt of Vincent Ogé in 1790, France granted citizenship to free people of colour in May 1791. White planters refused to comply, fighting between the groups broke out, and on 21 August 1791 the enslaved rose.

When France declared war on Britain in 1793, the grands blancs asked British help, and Britain invaded Saint-Domingue, as did Spain. The French commissioners Sonthonax and Étienne Polverel offered freedom to enslaved people who would fight for them and in 1793 proclaimed abolition in the colony's provinces. On 6 May 1794 Toussaint Louverture turned from the Spanish to the French. The British sent about 30,000 men in 1795 but suffered heavily from disease, and at least three of every five British troops sent between 1791 and 1797 died of it. The British left Port-au-Prince on 18 May 1798, and Toussaint defeated the forces of Rigaud in the War of the South, taking Jacmel on 11 March 1800.

A French expedition arrived at Le Cap on 2 February 1802. Dessalines held the fort of Crête-à-Pierrot for about twenty days before slipping out on 24 March. Toussaint agreed to terms on 6 May 1802, was later seized and shipped to France, and died in prison at Fort-de-Joux. French plans to restore slavery brought a new revolt in the summer of 1802, while yellow fever killed about 10,000 French by mid-July and the commander Leclerc in November. After war between France and Britain resumed on 18 May 1803, the Royal Navy blockaded the colony. On 30 November 1803, 8,000 French soldiers boarded British ships under terms agreed with Dessalines.

On 1 January 1804 Dessalines declared Haiti a free republic. From February until 22 April 1804, on his order, the remaining white colonists were massacred. France recognised independence in 1825 only on condition that Haiti pay an indemnity of 150 million francs to former slaveholders. Estimates of the dead vary: Robert Scheina gave 350,000 Haitians and 50,000 European troops, and the Encyclopedia of African American Politics nearly 200,000 Black people and as many as 100,000 French and British soldiers, with yellow fever the largest cause. Historians such as David Geggus judge the effect on slavery limited, while W. E. B. Du Bois held that it made British abolition easier.
hajj: The word ḥajj is similar to the Hebrew ḥag, 'festival', from the same Semitic root; the Hebrew term referred to the three pilgrimage festivals Israelites made to the Temple in Jerusalem each year. The present pattern of Hajj was established by Muhammad, but according to the Quran, elements of it trace back to Abraham. In Islamic tradition Abraham left his wife Hajar and his son Ishmael in the desert of ancient Mecca. Hajar ran seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwah looking for water, and a spring then rose beneath Ishmael's foot. Abraham was later commanded to build the Kaaba with Ishmael's help and to invite people to make pilgrimage there. The Quran refers to these events in verses 2:124–127 and 22:27–30.

Hajj is an annual pilgrimage to Mecca and one of the Five Pillars of Islam. It is a once-in-a-lifetime duty for every Muslim who is physically and financially able to make the journey and to support their family during their absence. Its rites are carried out over five to six days, from the 8th to the 12th or 13th of Dhu'l-Hijja, the last month of the Islamic calendar. Because that calendar is lunar, the Gregorian date moves each year, and the season falls twice in one Gregorian year about every 33 years.

The pilgrim enters the sacred state of ihram, wearing unstitched white clothing, and walks seven times counterclockwise around the Kaaba, an act called tawaf, then walks seven times between Safa and Marwah. On 9 Dhu'l-Hijja, the Day of Arafah, pilgrims stand in vigil on the plain of Arafat, about 20 km east of Mecca, from noon until sunset; a pilgrim's Hajj is considered invalid without this. They spend a night at Muzdalifah, and on 10 Dhu'l-Hijja at Mina they throw seven stones at the largest of three pillars representing Satan.

After the sacrifice of an animal, pilgrims shave or trim their hair, and the festival of Eid al-Adha follows. The shorter pilgrimage to Mecca, Umrah, can be made at other times of the year but does not replace the Hajj.
hakodate: Hakodate stands at the centre of the Kameda Peninsula in southern Hokkaido and is overlooked by Mount Hakodate. The region was originally populated by the Ainu, and the name Hakodate may derive from an Ainu word, hak-casi, meaning shallow fort.

Hakodate was founded in 1454, when Kono Kaganokami Masamichi built a large manor house in the fishing village of Usukeshi. His son Kono Suemichi was driven out into Kameda during an Ainu rebellion in 1512. In 1741 the Matsumae clan moved its Kameda magistracy to Masamichi's house in Hakodate. The Tokugawa shogunate took direct control of the town in 1779, which brought rapid development under the merchant Takadaya Kahei, honoured as the founder of its port. The Matsumae clan was restored to full power in 1821.

Under the Convention of Kanagawa, negotiated by Commodore Matthew C. Perry, Hakodate became in 1854 the first Japanese port opened to foreign trade, and it was fully opened on 2 June 1859 as one of five open ports of the 1858 Treaty of Amity and Commerce signed with the U.S.. From the Russian consulate Nicholas of Japan is credited with introducing Eastern Orthodox Christianity to Japan in 1861.

Hakodate was central to the Boshin War. The shogunate rebel Enomoto Takeaki fled there in the winter of 1868 with the remnants of his navy and a handful of French advisers, and they proclaimed the Republic of Ezo on 25 December. It failed to win international recognition. The rebels held the European-style Goryōkaku fort, and the naval Battle of Hakodate, fought from 4 to 10 May 1869, was a decisive victory for the Imperial Japanese Navy. Government forces defeated the secessionists and the fort and city were surrendered.

Hakodate is a port city in Oshima Subprefecture, Hokkaido, and the third largest in the island. It was the biggest city in Hokkaido until a fire on 21 March 1934 destroyed about two thirds of its buildings. The former Goryōkaku fort is now a public park, popular for cherry blossom viewing, and the foreign settlement, Orthodox church and other missionary churches are legacies of the port's opening.
halberstadt: Halberstadt received market rights from King Otto III in 989 and became the administrative centre of the Saxon Harzgau. Its bishops had the Church of Our Lady built from about 1005. In 1179 the forces of Henry the Lion devastated the town in his conflict with Emperor Frederick Barbarossa, and after Henry's fall the diocese became a prince-bishopric about 1180. The cathedral was rebuilt from 1236 and consecrated in 1491. Halberstadt joined a league of towns with Quedlinburg and Aschersleben in 1326, and from 1387 it was a member of the Hanse.

The citizens turned Protestant around 1540, and in 1566 the cathedral chapter elected the first Lutheran bishop, Prince Henry Julius of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel. Wallenstein's troops occupied the town in 1629. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 secularised the prince-bishopric into the Principality of Halberstadt, held by Brandenburg-Prussia, and the town became part of the Kingdom of Prussia in 1701. From 1747 the official and poet Johann Wilhelm Ludwig Gleim made his house an intellectual centre of the German Enlightenment. It is now the Gleimhaus museum.

Halberstadt's Jewish community is recorded from the 13th century. Berend Lehmann founded a beth midrash, the Klaus, in 1703 and financed a Baroque synagogue completed in 1712, and the town had one of the largest Jewish communities in central Europe. The synagogue was burned in the pogrom of 9 November 1938. After local Nazi leaders refused to surrender, 218 American bombers dropped 595 tons of bombs on the centre on 8 April 1945. About 2,500 people were killed and most of the old town was reduced to rubble.

Halberstadt is now a town in Saxony-Anhalt and the capital of Harz district. Its cathedral is notable among those of northern Europe for keeping its medieval treasury almost complete, including the oldest surviving tapestries in Europe, from the 12th century. About 450 timber-framed houses stand in the centre, and the Klaus houses the Moses Mendelssohn Academy. A performance of John Cage's organ piece As Slow As Possible began in the Burchardikirche in 2001 and is scheduled to last 639 years.
halifax-nova-scotia: The area was called Chebucto until Halifax was established in 1749 by Governor Edward Cornwallis, who named it in honour of George Montagu-Dunk, 2nd Earl of Halifax. The Mi'kmaq name for the harbour is K'jipuktuk or Chebookt, meaning Chief Harbour or Great Harbour. They called the Halifax Peninsula, with the downtown area and Point Pleasant Park, Amntu'kati, and the hillside where the town was established was known, according to Thomas Raddall, as Goo-ow-ak-a-de, place of many pines.

Before 1749 the Colony of Nova Scotia had been administered from Annapolis Royal, near the western opening of the Bay of Fundy. In 1749 King George II ordered Cornwallis to establish Halifax as a new capital. Equipped with 13 transports and a sloop of war, Cornwallis founded the Town of Halifax on what is now the Halifax Peninsula on 21 June 1749. The original grid plan devised at the founding included a central military parade square, the Grand Parade, which has City Hall at one end and hosts the annual Remembrance Day ceremony at its cenotaph. The fortress of Citadel Hill overlooks the downtown.

Halifax is the capital and most populous municipality of Nova Scotia, and the most populous in Atlantic Canada. The Halifax Regional Municipality consists of four former municipalities amalgamated in 1996: Halifax, Dartmouth, Bedford and Halifax County. In the 2021 census 348,634 people lived in its urban area, which surrounds Halifax Harbour. The Port of Halifax and Dalhousie University are among its major employers, and the Royal Canadian Navy has major installations along the harbour. The Canadian Museum of Immigration at Pier 21, an immigrant entry point prominent through the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s, opened as a National Historic Site in 1999.
hallein: Hallein is the capital of Hallein district in the Tennengau region. The town stretches along the Salzach river in the shadow of the Untersberg massif, close to the German border on the west. The municipal area includes the cadastral communities of Adnet II, Au, Burgfried, Dürrnberg, Gamp, Gries, Hallein proper, Oberalm II and Taxach. It is linked to the city of Salzburg by the suburban S-Bahn railway and by the A 10 Tauern Autobahn.

The area is known for the Hallein Salt Mine on the Dürrnberg plateau, and settlement has been traced back 4,000 years. A Celtic community lived there from 600 BCE until the Romans took over its Noricum kingdom in 15 BCE. In the middle of the 8th century Duke Tassilo III of Bavaria granted the estates to the Salzburg diocese, and from 987 they were held by St Peter's Abbey. Salt became crucial to the wealth of the Archbishopric of Salzburg, competing with the production of Reichenhall in Bavaria. Salt mining is first mentioned in a deed of 1198, and the name Hallein is documented from the early 13th century.

Beer brewing became common from the 15th century, and in 1489 Prince-Archbishop Leonhard von Keutschach acquired a large brewery whose Hofbräu Kaltenhausen beers became another main source of revenue. At the end of the 17th century Prince-Archbishop Kuenburg had the Protestant miners expelled, and several hundred of them emigrated to Walcheren and Zeelandic Flanders. Hallein became part of the Austrian Empire by 1816. In World War II the town had a work camp annex to the Dachau concentration camp, and afterwards a camp for displaced persons, Beth Israel, which closed in 1954.

Hallein is a historic town with about 21,150 inhabitants and the second largest in the state of Salzburg. The Keltenmuseum shows the Hallstatt and La Tène Celtic cultures and the development of salt mining through the Middle Ages and Renaissance. The Silent Night Museum documents the life of the composer Franz Xaver Gruber, who lived locally, and holds the guitar used by the lyricist Joseph Mohr.
halmahera: Halmahera, formerly known as Jilolo, Gilolo or Jailolo, has a land area of 17,780 square kilometres and is the seventh largest island of Indonesia. It is a volcanic island on an island arc that includes the Raja Ampat Islands, all uplifted by the northward movement of Australia and the subduction of the Pacific Plate. Dukono is an active volcano at the northern end of the island and Mount Ibu another on its northwest coast. Ultramafic rocks and ophiolites form the bedrock over large areas of the eastern peninsula. The flightless invisible rail and the palm Jailoloa halmaherensis are found only on the island.

Sparsely populated Halmahera has long had its fortunes tied to those of the smaller islands of Ternate and Tidore off its west coast. It was the site of the Sultanate of Jailolo, one of the four kingdoms of Maluku, the Maloko Kië Raha, with Ternate, Tidore and Bacan, in the era before the Dutch East India Company colonized the whole archipelago. The north of the island was the base of the Loloda Kingdom, one of the earlier Moluccan kingdoms of the 13th century, though it was not counted among the four prominent ones.

The naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace visited Halmahera, as he described in his book The Malay Archipelago (1869). In February 1858, on Ternate or perhaps on Halmahera itself, between bouts of fever, he arrived at the idea of natural selection, wrote it down over the next couple of days and sent the letter to Darwin.

During World War II the island was the site of a Japanese naval base at Kao Bay. In 1999 and 2000 a dispute between the mainly Christian district of Kao and the wholly Muslim district of Malifut grew into religious fighting that spread through much of the North Moluccas, and thousands of people on Halmahera were killed.

Sofifi, the capital of North Maluku province, stands on the west coast of Halmahera, opposite Tidore; the provincial government moved there from Ternate in 2010. In that year the island itself had a population of 449,938, and about half of its inhabitants are Muslim and half Christian. Tobelo is the largest town. The coast is inhabited by the Tobelo people, while the Togutil, a small semi-nomadic related people of the interior, are estimated at 1,500 to 3,000 people.
hama: The ancient settlement of Hamath was occupied from the early Neolithic to the Iron Age. After the fall of the Hittite Empire it was the capital of a Syro-Hittite kingdom known from the Hebrew Bible, which traded with Israel and Judah. In 853 BCE its king Irhuleni and Hadadezer of Aram-Damascus led a coalition against the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III at the Battle of Qarqar, a battle that seems to have been closer to a draw. Around 720 BCE Sargon II razed the city after a failed revolt, resettled it with 6,300 Assyrians and had its king flayed alive in Assyria.

Under the Seleucids the city was renamed Epiphaneia after Antiochus IV Epiphanes, and the Romans annexed Syria in 64 BCE. Five hundred Hamian archers were stationed on Hadrian's Wall from 120 CE. Muslim forces under Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah took the city in 638 or 639, and it regained its old name. The Crusader Tancred took it in 1108, but the Seljuks recovered it in 1114. Two earthquakes in 1157 shattered it, and Nur al-Din rebuilt its walls and, in 1172, its Great Mosque.

Saladin took Hama in 1175 and gave it four years later to his nephew al-Muzaffar Umar, beginning Ayyubid rule that lasted almost continuously until 1342. The Mongols sacked it in 1260. The historian and geographer Abu al-Fida governed the city from 1310 to 1332. Ibn Battuta visited in 1335. The Ottomans conquered it in 1516. It became part of the French Mandate of Syria after 1918, and a rising took place in the city in 1925 during the Great Syrian Revolt.

Hama lies on the Orontes 213 kilometres north of Damascus and is the capital of the Hama Governorate. Its seventeen norias, water wheels up to 20 metres across, were used for irrigation and now serve as a symbol of the city. In February 1982 government forces under the president's brother Rifaat al-Assad put down an Islamist revolt in the city, shelling quarters held by the insurgents and razing part of the old city. Government forces are alleged to have executed thousands of prisoners and civilians afterwards.
hamadan: Hamadan lies in the foothills of Alvand Mountain in midwestern Iran, at about 1,850 metres above sea level and some 360 kilometres south-west of Tehran. It is the capital of Hamadan province and is believed to be among the oldest Iranian cities. Classical sources call it Ecbatana, from Old Persian Hamgmatāna. The Ganj Nameh inscription and the monuments to Avicenna and Baba Taher are its main sights.

The city may conceivably, though improbably, be mentioned in cuneiform texts of about 1100 BCE from the time of the Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser I, according to Clifford Edmund Bosworth. It is certainly mentioned by Herodotus, who says that the king of Media, Diokes, built Ecbatana in the 7th century BCE. It later became one of several capitals of the Achaemenid dynasty. The book of Ezra says that at Ecbatana a scroll was found that gave the Jews permission from King Darius to rebuild the temple in Jerusalem.

Under the Parthians, whose capital was Ctesiphon, Hamadan was the summer capital, and the Sasanians built summer palaces there. After the Battle of Nahavand in 642 it fell to the Arabs. In 931 Mardavij, founder of the Al-Ziyar dynasty, plundered it after its people killed his nephew. The Seljuks took the last Kakuyid fortress in 1047 and later moved their capital from Baghdad to Hamadan. The Mongols destroyed it in 1220, and the Timurid invasions destroyed it again, but it thrived in the Safavid era. Benjamin of Tudela reported 30,000 Jews there in 1170.

In the 18th century the city was surrendered to the Ottomans and returned to Iran through the work of Nader Shah. During the First World War Russian, Ottoman and British forces fought over it and occupied it in turn. Avicenna entered the city when it was the capital of the Buyid dynasty, taught at its great school and completed many of his writings there.
hamamatsu: Hamamatsu lies in western Shizuoka Prefecture, 260 kilometres south-west of Tokyo, between Lake Hamana to the west, the Tenryū River to the east and the Pacific Ocean to the south. It has a flat plain and the Mikatahara Plateau in the south and mountains in the north. The area has been settled since prehistoric times, and the Shijimizuka shell mound and the Akamonue Kofun tomb survive from the Jōmon and Kofun periods.

In the Nara period it became the capital of Tōtōmi Province. In the Sengoku period Hamamatsu Castle was the home of the future shōgun Tokugawa Ieyasu. The city flourished in the Edo period under a succession of daimyō as a castle town and a post town on the Tōkaidō highway between Edo and Kyoto. The Hamamatsu Kite Festival, held each May, is said to have begun about 430 years ago, when the lord of the castle marked the birth of his first son by flying kites.

After the Meiji Restoration Hamamatsu was a prefecture from 1871 to 1876 before it was united with Shizuoka Prefecture. The station opened on the Tōkaidō Main Line in 1889, the same year it became a town, and it became a city on 1 July 1911. An Army air base opened in 1926 and a flight school in 1933. The Tonankai earthquake of 7 December 1944 caused much damage, and US air raids largely destroyed the city in June 1945.

Hamamatsu is the largest city in Shizuoka Prefecture, with an estimated 780,128 inhabitants in 2023,. It is known as an industrial city, above all for musical instruments and motorcycles. Honda was founded there, and Yamaha, Suzuki, Kawai and Roland have headquarters in the city. A 1990 change in Japanese immigration law drew a large Brazilian Nikkei population to work in its factories. The Hamamatsu International Piano Competition has been held every three years since 1991, and the Museum of Musical Instruments opened in 1995.
hamburg: Hamburg lies at a sheltered natural harbour on the southern fanning-out of the Jutland Peninsula, between continental Europe to the south and Scandinavia to the north, with the North Sea to the west and the Baltic Sea to the northeast. It stands on the River Elbe at its confluence with the Alster and Bille, where the 110 km Elbe estuary begins. The city centre is around the Binnenalster and Außenalster, both lakes formed by damming the Alster. The Altes Land, part of the city, is the largest contiguous fruit-producing region in Central Europe.

Claudius Ptolemy, in the 2nd century CE, reported the first name for the vicinity as Treva. The name Hamburg comes from the first permanent building on the site, a castle which Charlemagne ordered built in 808. It rose on rocky terrain in a marsh between the Alster and the Elbe as a defence against Slavic incursion and acquired the name Hammaburg, burg meaning castle or fort.

In 834 Hamburg became the seat of a bishopric, whose first bishop, Ansgar, later known as the Apostle of the North, founded the city's early Christian institutions. Two years later it was linked with Bremen to form the Bishopric of Hamburg-Bremen. The town was destroyed repeatedly in its early centuries. In 845 a fleet of 600 Viking ships sailed up the Elbe and destroyed it, when it had about 500 inhabitants. King Mieszko II Lambert of Poland burned it in 1030, and Valdemar II of Denmark raided and occupied it in 1201 and 1214. The Black Death reached Hamburg in 1350 and killed at least 60 per cent of its population, and the city suffered several major fires in the medieval period.

Hamburg was a member of the Hanseatic League and a free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire. Before the unification of Germany in 1871 it was a fully sovereign city state, and before 1919 it was a civic republic headed constitutionally by a class of hereditary Grand Burghers, or Hanseaten. Later disasters included the Great Fire of 1842, the Allied fire-bombing of 1943 and the North Sea flood of 1962.

Officially the Free and Hanseatic City of Hamburg, it is the second-largest city in Germany after Berlin and one of the country's three city-states, with Berlin and Bremen. Its population is over 1.9 million. The Port of Hamburg is Germany's largest. The Speicherstadt and Kontorhausviertel were declared World Heritage Sites by UNESCO in 2015.
hammurabi: Hammurabi was the sixth Amorite king of Babylon and the son of Sin-muballit. His reign came after the fall of the Third Dynasty of Ur in 2004 BCE, when Mesopotamia was divided among several kingdoms ruled by Amorite dynasties, of which Isin and then Larsa were the strongest in the south. Babylon had been a secondary city until an Amorite dynasty took root there around 1880 BCE with Sumu-la-El. Babylonian sources give Hammurabi a reign of 43 years. The first two decades are poorly documented, and the names of the years of that time refer chiefly to public works and offerings to the gods.

Elam, whose heartland lay in the south-west of present-day Iran, expanded into the Mesopotamian plain and subjugated Eshnunna. This led to war with a coalition of kingdoms that included Babylon and Mari, and the Elamites were eventually repelled with great difficulty with the help of troops from Mari and other northern kingdoms. Strengthened by this success, Hammurabi went on to conquer the kingdoms of Larsa, Eshnunna and Mari. Almost all of Mesopotamia came under Babylonian rule, so that it is possible to speak of an empire. His conquests seem to have come mainly from opportunities as they arose, not from a prepared imperial plan.

Hammurabi is best known for his law code, which is said to have been inspired by Shamash, the Babylonian god of justice. It was written towards the end of his reign and is known mainly from a large stele, which shows the king facing Shamash. It has a prologue, a set of provisions and an epilogue. It is not the only Mesopotamian legislative collection, nor the oldest, but it is the longest known. Its status is debated, and in its prologue and epilogue it presents itself as a commemorative inscription that celebrates his sense of justice. The prologue names the gods who bestow sovereignty, Enlil, Marduk and Ishtar, and his descent from the founder of his dynasty.

Hammurabi also carried out public works. The 33rd year of his reign commemorates a canal named in his honour, which gave perennial water to Nippur, Eridu, Ur, Larsa, Uruk and Isin. He rebuilt sanctuaries, including the ziggurat of Zababa at Kish. Letters found at Mari and at Larsa, more than 200 of the latter addressed to his subordinates, make his the best documented of the Mesopotamian reigns. His son Samsu-iluna failed to maintain the empire. Hammurabi was later revered as a great conqueror, then chiefly as the ideal lawgiver, and archaeologists rediscovered him in the late 19th century. He is seen as an important figure in the history of law.
hampshire: Hampshire is bordered by Berkshire to the north, Surrey and West Sussex to the east, the Solent to the south, Dorset to the west and Wiltshire to the north-west. Undulating hills characterise much of it, with a belt of chalk running from the Hampshire Downs in the north-west to the South Downs in the south-east. The Loddon and Wey drain north into the Thames, while the Itchen and Test flow south into Southampton Water. The south-west holds the New Forest, one of the largest expanses of ancient woodland remaining in England. The county historically contained Bournemouth, Christchurch and the Isle of Wight.

The region is believed to have been continuously occupied since the end of the last Ice Age, its first inhabitants being Mesolithic hunter-gatherers concentrated around the river valleys. Hampshire was incorporated into the Roman province of Britannia soon after the invasion of 43 CE, and its political leaders are generally believed to have accepted this peacefully. Its chief town, Venta Belgarum, now Winchester, became capital of the Belgae. A fortification near Southampton, Clausentum, belonged to the Saxon Shore forts, and a New Forest pottery industry exported widely across southern Britain. The West Saxons moved south in the late seventh century and incorporated Hampshire into their kingdom. The name is attested as Hamtunscir in 755, from the Saxon settlement of Hamtun, now Southampton.

After the Norman Conquest London became the capital, but Winchester remained important, and the New Forest was a prized royal hunting forest, where King William Rufus was killed while hunting in 1100. The Domesday Book of 1086 records 44 hundreds. From the 12th century the ports grew with trade, wool and cloth, fishing and shipbuilding, and by 1523 at the latest Southampton had outstripped Winchester in population. In the two world wars the county played a crucial military role through the Royal Navy base at Portsmouth, the army camp at Aldershot and Netley Hospital. Supermarine, designer of the Spitfire, was based in Southampton, which led to severe bombing of the city in the Second World War.

Hampshire is a ceremonial county in South East England with an area of 3,769 square kilometres and Southampton as its largest settlement. Portsmouth lies in the south-east, Winchester in the centre, and Basingstoke and Andover in the north. Hampshire County Council sits at Castle Hill in Winchester. Its county day is 15 July, St Swithun's Day. The Hambledon Club, formed about 1750, created many of cricket's early laws, and the Battle of Cheriton was fought near Winchester in 1644.
han-chinese: Han Chinese trace their ancestry and culture to the Huaxia, a confederation of agricultural tribes of the late Neolithic and early Bronze Age that lived along the Guanzhong and Yellow River basins in northern China. Early Chinese history is largely mythical: Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian records successive overlords, the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors, for whom little reliable archaeological evidence exists. The name Han people first appeared during the Northern and Southern period and was inspired by the Han dynasty, and the Chinese language and script came to be called the Han language and Han characters.

Qin and Han rule sent settlers south. Qin Shi Huang is said to have sent several hundred thousand men and fifteen thousand women to settle Lingnan under a general named Zhao Tuo, and the Han emperor Wu later ordered a further two hundred thousand men to build ships to attack and colonize the region. Successive migrations southward fused the newcomers with the peoples south of the Yangtze, while the centres of Han wealth and culture moved from the Yellow River basin to Jiangnan. By the Tang and Song dynasties the Han were the main inhabitants of the fertile lowlands and cities of the south.

Han Chinese have often held the dominant positions of governance, but dynastic rule was in notable periods held by others, among them the Liao (916–1125), the Jin (1115–1234), the Yuan (1271–1368) and the Qing (1644–1912). Sun Yat-sen made the restoration of Han rule a tenet of the 1911 Revolution, which overthrew the Manchu-led Qing and established the Han-dominated Republic of China.

Scholars such as Kevin Carrico and Dru Gladney argue that a single Han identity, set against Manchu rulers, is a modern development promoted by nationalists near the end of the Qing. Liang Qichao coined the term Zhonghua minzu between 1902 and 1905 to refer to the Han; it later became a wider concept for all the peoples of China. Han Chinese make up about 91 percent of the population of China. Their literary heritage includes the Analects, the Tao Te Ching and the Four Great Classical Novels.
han-dynasty: The Han dynasty was established by Liu Bang after the short-lived Qin dynasty collapsed within four years of the death of Qin Shi Huang. Two former rebel leaders, Xiang Yu of Chu and Liu Bang of Han, fought for hegemony, and Liu Bang defeated Xiang Yu at the Battle of Gaixia in 202 BCE. He took the title of emperor and is known after death as Emperor Gaozu. Chang'an, modern Xi'an, became the capital. The dynasty took its name from Hanzhong, the small fief on the Han River that Xiang Yu had given Liu Bang. The Western Han lasted until 9 CE, and the Eastern Han formally began on 5 August 25 CE, when Liu Xiu became Emperor Guangwu.

The Xiongnu defeated the Han in 200 BCE, and the court responded with marriage alliances and payments of tribute. Emperor Wu changed this policy in 133 BCE with a series of campaigns that took the Hexi Corridor and the Tarim Basin from the Xiongnu, helping to establish the Silk Road. He also annexed Nanyue in 111 BCE and Dian in 109 BCE, and in 108 BCE Han forces conquered Gojoseon and set up the Xuantu and Lelang commanderies in Korea. From his reign onward the court sponsored Confucianism, and in 124 BCE he established the Imperial University. To finance his campaigns he nationalised the salt and iron industries in 117 BCE, monopolies repealed under the Eastern Han.

Wang Mang, regent after the death of Emperor Ai, interrupted the dynasty with his Xin dynasty from 9 to 23 CE. After 92 CE palace eunuchs became involved in violent power struggles with the consort clans of the empresses. The Yellow Turban and Five Pecks of Rice rebellions, led by Taoist religious societies, challenged imperial authority in 184. After the death of Emperor Ling in 189 the eunuchs were massacred by military officers, and governors became warlords who divided the empire. The dynasty ended in 220 when Cao Pi, king of Wei, usurped the throne from Emperor Xian.

The emperor stood at the apex of society and was in theory unlimited in power, but ministers pressed him through institutions such as the court conference, and emperors were often minors ruled over by a regent. Below him came the kings of the Liu clan, and the empire was divided into provinces, commanderies and counties, plus semi-autonomous kingdoms that lost autonomy after the Rebellion of the Seven States. Taxes were paid in coin, and the poll tax stimulated a money economy. Han technology included papermaking, which the Han tradition credits to Cai Lun in 105, rudders, raised-relief maps and seismometers. Today the majority ethnic group of China calls itself the Han people.
han-fei: Han Fei was born into the ruling family of the State of Han in the last phase of the Warring States period, which made him unlike most philosophers of his age, who came from outside the aristocracy. Scholars place his birth at about 280 BCE, though the exact year is unknown. Some have read his writings as addressed to his cousin, the King of Han. The Records of the Grand Historian, compiled by Sima Qian, say that he studied alongside the future Qin chancellor Li Si under the Confucian philosopher Xun Kuang, and that a stutter kept him from presenting his ideas in court, though he wrote with great skill.

The Han Feizi is a later anthology traditionally attributed to him. Sima Qian lists among its essays Solitary Indignation, Five Vermin, Inner and Outer Congeries of Sayings, Collected Persuasions and Difficulties in the Way of Persuasion, which he puts at about one hundred thousand words. Modern scholars differ over how much of the book is his; the sinologist Goldin has held that the outline of his life is probably not far from the truth, while Masayuki Sato doubted that all of Sima Qian's details are accurate.

Han Fei drew together the methods of earlier thinkers: Shang Yang's emphasis on laws, Shen Buhai's on administrative technique and Shen Dao's on authority. A ruler who mastered position or power (shi), technique (shu) and law (fa) could, in his view, hold firm control of the state. He stressed holding actual outcomes accountable to speech, joined to a system of two handles, punishment and reward. Like his teacher Xun Kuang he took human nature to be without virtue, but he proposed to steer people through their own self-interest rather than through moral education.

According to Sima Qian, King Ying Zheng of Qin read Han Fei's works and said that if he could meet their author he might die without regrets. Han Fei came to the Qin court and presented an essay asking the king not to attack Han. Yao Gu and Li Si used it to have him imprisoned on grounds of probable loyalty to his homeland, and Li Si then forced him to drink poison. The Qin king afterwards regretted his death. A different account, in the Stratagems of the Warring States, has the king order his execution after he slandered the Qin diplomat Yao Jia.

After the early fall of the Qin dynasty, the succeeding Han dynasty officially vilified the Legalist school. Even so, its ideas continued to influence later dynasties, and Han Fei's thought is sometimes compared with that of Niccolò Machiavelli.
hanafi-school: The Hanafi school emerged from the legal tradition of Kufa in Iraq, where Abu Hanifa lived and where jurists were known for independent reasoning, or ra'y. Abu Hanifa attended the study circle of Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman for about twenty years and inherited it at Hammad's death. He and his students systematised ra'y and the method of analogical reasoning, qiyās. Where qiyās gave an unsuitable result, early Hanafis used juristic discretion, istiḥsān. There is no record of treatises by Abu Hanifa himself. His teachings were passed on by his disciples Abu Yusuf and Muhammad al-Shaybani. Traditionists accused the Hanafis of preferring ra'y to hadith, and al-Shafi'i criticised istiḥsān as subjective.

The school won the support of the Abbasid state, which wished to unify the legal system and preferred Hanafi judges. Abu Yusuf served as a judge in Baghdad, and Harun al-Rashid later appointed him chief judge. In the 9th century the school changed from a personal school around individual jurists into a legal community with a doctrine handed down from teachers to students. It became the prevailing school in Transoxiana, especially under the Samanids, and this region was a centre of classical Hanafi scholarship from the 10th to the 12th centuries. It gave rise to the Maturidi school of theology.

The Seljuk rulers favoured the eastern Hanafis and appointed them to official posts, and in the 11th and 12th centuries the Hanafi and Maturidi schools spread west into Syria, Anatolia and western Persia. The Ottoman Empire adopted the school as its official school of law, and by the 16th century the Şeyḫülislâm was chief religious and judicial authority. Between 1869 and 1877 the Ottomans issued the Mecelle, a codification of Hanafi jurisprudence.

In India the Mughal emperor Awrangzib ordered the compilation of Hanafi fatwas, completed between 1664 and 1672 as the al-Fatawa l-ʿAlamgiriyya. The East India Company later based Anglo-Muhammadan law partly on a translation of the Hidaya. The Hanafi school is the largest of the four main Sunni schools. It is estimated at around 800 million followers, about 45 per cent of Muslims, and predominates in the Balkans, Central Asia, the Caucasus, Turkey, the Levant and South Asia.
hanging-gardens-of-babylon: The gardens were described as an ascending series of tiered gardens holding a wide variety of trees, shrubs and vines, resembling a large green mountain built of mud bricks. The Greek word behind the name, kremastos, means overhanging and refers to trees planted on a raised structure such as a terrace. They were said to stand in the city of Babylon, near present-day Hillah in Iraq's Babil province.

According to one legend, they were built beside a palace called the Marvel of Mankind for the Median wife of Nebuchadnezzar II, Queen Amytis, who missed the green hills and valleys of her homeland. The Babylonian priest Berossus, writing about 290 BCE, gave this account, and Josephus later quoted it. The gardens have also been attributed to the queen Semiramis, a figure of legend.

Five classical writers describe them in some form. Berossus is the earliest known mention and the only source to credit Nebuchadnezzar II. Diodorus Siculus, probably drawing on Cleitarchus and Ctesias of Cnidus, speaks of a Syrian king and gives a square garden with sides of about four plethra and an uppermost gallery 50 cubits high, watered from the Euphrates. Quintus Curtius Rufus places the gardens on a citadel and also names a Syrian king. Strabo says the water was raised by a screw, as does Philo of Byzantium, who praises the engineering of so much deep soil raised above the surrounding land.

No surviving Babylonian text mentions the gardens, and Nebuchadnezzar's long inscriptions do not mention any garden, nor his wife Amytis. No archaeological evidence has been found at Babylon. It is possible that traces lie beneath the Euphrates, which flowed east of its present course in his time, and little is known about the western part of the city. Herodotus describes Babylon without mentioning them. Three explanations have been offered: that they were a poetic ideal of an eastern garden, that they existed and were destroyed around the first century CE, or that the tradition refers to another place.

The Oxford scholar Stephanie Dalley proposes that they were the gardens Sennacherib (reigned c. 705/704 to c. 681 BCE) built at his palace in Nineveh. Sennacherib's inscriptions call the palace and garden a wonder for all peoples and describe water screws. An aqueduct at Jerwan, built of over two million dressed stones, carried water to Nineveh, and a wall panel of his grandson Assurbanipal shows the garden in maturity. Dalley suggests that the two cities became confused over the centuries; the garden's position at Nineveh has not been confirmed.
hangul: Before Hangul, Korea had used Hanja, Chinese characters, since antiquity. The script was difficult, which limited its use mostly to the upper class and left commoners largely illiterate, and it was poorly suited to a language not closely related to Chinese: Korean pronunciation and ideas could be represented only indirectly. The Joseon king Sejong the Great, who reigned from 1418 to 1450, was responsible for Hangul's creation, and most scholars believe he was personally and significantly involved.

Because records are lacking, it is unknown when work began or what the process was. The script was first introduced, probably in a mostly complete form, to Sejong's court in the 12th month of 1443 of the Korean calendar, roughly 30 December 1443 to 28 January 1444. It was officially published in 1446 in the text Hunminjeongeum and its companion commentary, the Haerye. Part of the effort that followed produced the Yongbiŏch'ŏn'ga, the first work of Hangul literature.

The original name, Hunminjeongeum, means 'Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People'. Modern Korean orthographies use 24 basic letters, called jamo: 14 consonants and 10 vowels. Combinations bring the total to 51. The letters are arranged in syllable blocks made of an initial consonant, a vowel and an optional final consonant. Linguists classify the script as a phonographic alphabet, and some have called it a featural script, one in which letter shapes encode features of speech.

The letters were designed to be graphically simple, traditionally of only straight lines, dots and circles. The shapes of five basic consonants are based on those of the human speech organs, and most of the other basic consonants are derived from them by adding lines to show progressively harsher sounds.
