Sejong tried to spread Hangul through government and society with limited success. In the 15th century it was rarely used, mainly in Seoul among people close to the court, and it began to spread beyond Seoul in the 16th century. Women and Buddhists were significant early adopters, and women often taught it at home, though it was rarely taught in Confucian curricula. The elite looked down on it for centuries.

After Korea ended its isolation in the 1870s the script came to be seen as a symbol of national identity, and reform movements, together called the Hangul Movement, arose. Under Japanese colonial rule from 1910 its use was repressed to varying degrees, and it expanded after the 1919 March First Movement. After 1945 usage diverged in the two Koreas; North Korea's Compendium of Korean Language Norms appeared in 1966 and South Korea's Hangeul Orthography in 1989. Hangul is now the predominant script for Korean.
hangzhou: Hangzhou lies in northwestern Zhejiang province, at the southern end of the Grand Canal, which runs to Beijing, in the south-central part of the Yangtze River Delta. The city centre is built around the eastern and northern sides of West Lake, just north of the Qiantang River, the largest river in Zhejiang. Each year a tidal bore races up the Qiantang through Hangzhou, reaching up to 12 m in height. The climate is humid subtropical, with long, hot, humid summers and chilly, drier winters.

The Hemudu culture inhabited Yuyao, 100 km south-east of Hangzhou, as far back as seven thousand years ago, when rice was first cultivated in southeast China. The jade-carving Liangzhu culture, named for its type site just northwest of the city, lived in the surrounding area around five thousand years ago. Hangzhou was established as a county seat in 221 BCE and later served as the capital of the Wuyue Kingdom (923 to 997).

Under the Tang dynasty the poet Bai Juyi, as governor, had a stronger and taller dyke built to hold the water of West Lake, which the surrounding farmland depended on, and had willows planted along it. In 1089 another poet-governor, Su Shi, used 200,000 workers to build a 2.8 km causeway across the lake from mud dredged from its bottom.

Hangzhou became the capital of the Southern Song dynasty after the Jurchens conquered most of northern China and captured Kaifeng in the Jingkang Incident of 1127. The surviving imperial family had retreated south, and Emperor Gaozong moved from Nanjing to Shangqiu to Yangzhou before settling at Hangzhou. The city was besieged and captured by the Mongol armies of Kublai Khan in 1276. The historian Patricia Buckley Ebrey noted that the Mongols spared Hangzhou and the Zhao royal family of the Southern Song, while they had killed the Jurchen Wanyan royal family by the hundreds at the Siege of Kaifeng in 1232. The new Yuan capital was Dadu (Beijing), but Hangzhou remained an important commercial and administrative centre for the south.

The port remained important until the middle of the Ming dynasty, when its harbour slowly silted up. Under the Qing it held an imperial army garrison. The Taiping Heavenly Kingdom occupied the city in 1856 and 1860, and it was heavily damaged in its conquest, occupation and reconquest by the Qing army.

Hangzhou is the capital and most populous city of Zhejiang province and a sub-provincial city. Three UNESCO World Heritage Sites lie in or near it: the West Lake Cultural Landscape, the Grand Canal and the Archaeological Ruins of Liangzhu City. Its native residents speak the Hangzhou dialect, a Wu dialect, and its cuisine is regarded as representative of Zhejiang cooking.
hannah-arendt: Hannah Arendt was born Johanna Arendt in 1906 in Linden, Prussia, into a secular, educated and well-established Jewish family of merchants from Königsberg. Her father died when she was seven. Her mother, an ardent Social Democrat, raised her on strict Goethean lines, with the reading of Goethe's complete works. After secondary school in Berlin she studied at the University of Marburg under Martin Heidegger. She obtained her doctorate in philosophy at Heidelberg in 1929 under Karl Jaspers, with a dissertation on love in Augustine. In 1929 she also married Günther Stern, in Potsdam.

In 1933 the Gestapo briefly imprisoned Arendt for illegal research into antisemitism. She fled Germany with her mother, crossing the Ore Mountains by night into Czechoslovakia, and in Geneva she committed herself to the Jewish cause. She settled in Paris, where she worked for Youth Aliyah, helping young Jews emigrate to the British Mandate of Palestine. When Germany invaded France she was detained as an alien by the French government. She escaped and reached New York on 22 May 1941. There she became a writer and editor, worked for Jewish Cultural Reconstruction and became an American citizen in 1950. She taught at many American universities but declined tenure-track appointments.

The Origins of Totalitarianism of 1951, her first major book, examined the roots of Stalinism and Nazism in three essays: Antisemitism, Imperialism and Totalitarianism. The Human Condition of 1958 distinguishes political from social concepts, and labour from work, and develops a theory of political action in a public realm. Of human actions she singles out forgiving past wrong and promising future benefit. Between Past and Future collects eight essays written between 1954 and 1968, and her biography of Rahel Varnhagen, finished in 1938, was published in 1957.

Arendt never developed a systematic political theory and kept apart from schools of thought. The tradition most closely identified with her is civic republicanism, from Aristotle to Tocqueville, centred on active citizenship and collective deliberation. She is also remembered for the controversy over the trial of Adolf Eichmann and for the phrase the banality of evil. Her husband Heinrich Blücher died on 31 October 1970. She had a near-fatal heart attack while lecturing in Scotland in May 1974, and died of another in her New York apartment on 4 December 1975. Her ashes were buried beside Blücher's at Bard College, and her last work, The Life of the Mind, was left unfinished.
hannibal: Hannibal was one of the sons of the Carthaginian general and statesman Hamilcar Barca and an unknown mother, and was most likely born in Carthage. His name combines the name Hanno with the god Baal Hammon, and its exact vocalisation is debated. He had two brothers, Hasdrubal and Mago. His brothers-in-law, Hasdrubal the Fair and the Numidian king Naravas, were close associates of his father in the Mercenary War and the Punic conquest of the Iberian Peninsula. Rome's defeat of Carthage in the First Punic War had left deep tension, and Hannibal pledged to his father never to be a friend of Rome.

In 218 BCE Hannibal attacked Saguntum, an ally of Rome in Hispania, which sparked the Second Punic War. He invaded Italy by way of the Alps with North African war elephants, and about 10,000 Celtic tribesmen joined his army in the Po Valley. He won victories at Ticinus, Trebia, Lake Trasimene and Cannae. At Cannae in 216 BCE he seized the supply depot on the Apulian plain; the Roman army there is estimated by some at 100,000 but more likely 50,000 to 80,000.

The war then settled into a stalemate. Following the strategy of Fabius Maximus, called Cunctator, the Romans refused open battle and wore down Hannibal's army with smaller forces. Carthaginian defeats in Hispania prevented his reinforcement, and he held most of southern Italy for about 15 years without a decisive victory.

In 203 BCE a Roman invasion of North Africa under Scipio Africanus led to his recall to Carthage. At the Battle of Zama in 202 BCE the Romans had the superior cavalry, after King Masinissa of Numidia changed sides, while the Carthaginians had more infantry and 80 elephants. Hannibal was defeated, ending the war.

After the peace left Carthage with an indemnity of ten thousand talents, Hannibal was elected suffete, or chief magistrate. He reorganised the state's finances to end corruption and recover embezzled funds so that the indemnity could be paid without raising taxes. The reforms were unpopular with members of the Carthaginian aristocracy and in Rome, and he went into voluntary exile.

He served as a military adviser to Antiochus III the Great at the Seleucid court in his war with Rome. After Antiochus lost at the Battle of Magnesia, Hannibal fled again, stopping in Armenia and reaching the court of Bithynia. There he was betrayed to the Romans and died by suicide, poisoning himself.
hanoi: Hanoi lies on the Red River, whose curved course around the city was symbolised as a dragon. Several of the city's older names contain the Chinese word for dragon: it was first called Long Biên, then Tống Bình and Long Đỗ, and after its recapture in 866 by the Tang general Gao Pian it was renamed Đại La. Medieval Muslim sources between the 9th and 12th century called it Luqin, a term derived from Longbian.

Stone tools of the Sơn Vi culture, 10,000 to 20,000 years old, have been found at Ba Vì and Đông Anh. From about 10,000 to 4,000 years ago the area was under water as the sea rose, and the region is believed to have been inhabited continuously for the last 4,000 years.

Around the third century BCE a fortified citadel, later named Cổ Loa, was built in the area; it was the first political centre of the Vietnamese civilisation before Chinese influence, with an outer embankment covering 600 hectares. In 179 BCE Nanyue annexed the region, and Zhao Tuo left the indigenous chiefs in control of the population. For the first time the area formed part of a polity headed by a Chinese ruler.

In 1010, under the Lý dynasty, Emperor Lý Thái Tổ established the capital of Đại Việt in what later became central Hanoi and named it Thăng Long, meaning ascending dragon. In 1428 King Lê Lợi renamed it Đông Kinh, eastern capital, a name used until 1789. In 1802 the Nguyễn dynasty moved the national capital to Huế, and the city was renamed Hanoi in 1831. The French took control in 1888 and shaped the city's architecture to their tastes. Hanoi was the capital of the French protectorate of Tonkin from 1883 to 1949 and of French Indochina from 1902 to 1945. Ernest Hebrard drew up a development plan in 1924, which was partly carried out.

After the August Revolution and the fall of the Nguyễn dynasty, the Democratic Republic of Vietnam made Hanoi its capital. The city was part of the State of Vietnam from 1949 to 1954 and again of the Democratic Republic from 1954 to 1976. In 1976 it became the capital of the unified Socialist Republic of Vietnam.

Hanoi is the capital and second most populous centrally governed city of Vietnam, with about 8.7 million people. Its Old Quarter, near Hoàn Kiếm Lake, keeps most of its original street layout, descended from the 36 streets where merchants specialised in trades such as silk, jewellery or bamboo. The city also holds the Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long, the Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum and the French colonial Hanoi Opera House and St. Joseph's Cathedral. UNESCO gave Hanoi the title City for Peace on 16 July 1999.
hanover: Hanover lies at the confluence of the River Leine and its tributary the Ihme, in the south of the North German Plain and northwest of the Harz mountains. Its position at a natural crossroads and on the upper navigable reaches of the Leine shaped its growth. The river linked it to the Hanseatic League city of Bremen, and east-west traffic skirting the Harz between the Low Countries and Saxony or Thuringia passed through it.

Hanover was founded in medieval times on the east bank of the Leine. Its original name, Honovere, may mean high river bank, though this is debated. A small village of ferrymen and fishermen, it became a comparatively large town in the 13th century and received town privileges in 1241. It was the capital of the Principality of Calenberg from 1636 to 1692 and of the Electorate of Hanover from 1692 to 1814. From 1714 to 1837 it was by personal union the family seat of the Hanoverian kings of Great Britain and Ireland.

In July 1803 Napoleon imposed the Convention of Artlenburg, and about 35,000 French soldiers occupied the country. George III did not recognise the convention, and many Hanoverian soldiers emigrated to Britain, where the King's German Legion was formed; it later played a part in the Peninsular War and at Waterloo in 1815. The electorate became the Kingdom of Hanover in 1814. After 1866 Hanover was the capital of a province of Prussia, and the city passed 100,000 inhabitants in 1875. It lay in the British zone of occupation after the Second World War and became part of the new state of Lower Saxony in 1946.

Hanover is the capital and largest city of Lower Saxony, with a population of 535,932 in 2021. It is a major crossing of railway lines and motorways and one of the world's leading exhibition cities; its fairground, extended especially for Expo 2000, is the largest in the world, and the Hanover Fair has been held since 1947. The Great Garden of the Royal Gardens of Herrenhausen is an important European Baroque garden. The palace there was largely destroyed by Allied bombing and reopened after reconstruction in 2013.
hans-christian-andersen: Hans Christian Andersen was born in Odense on 2 April 1805. His father, also named Hans, had an elementary school education and introduced his son to literature by reading him the Arabian Nights; his mother, Anne Marie Andersdatter, was an illiterate washerwoman. After his father's death in 1816 the boy attended a local school for poor children and had to support himself, working as an apprentice to a weaver and later to a tailor.

At 14 he moved to Copenhagen to seek work as an actor and was accepted into the Royal Danish Theatre for his soprano voice, which soon broke. A colleague told him he considered him a poet, and Andersen turned to writing. Jonas Collin, the theatre's director, persuaded King Frederick VI to pay part of his schooling at Slagelse and later Elsinore, which lasted until 1827.

His first story, "The Ghost at Palnatoke's Grave", appeared in 1822. In 1829 he had considerable success with the short story "A Journey on Foot from Holmen's Canal to the East Point of Amager", followed by a play and a short volume of poems. A small travel grant from the king in 1833 let him begin the first of many journeys through Europe, and he reached Rome in October 1834. His travels in Italy shaped his first novel, The Improvisatore, a fictionalized autobiography published in 1835 to instant acclaim.

Andersen's first fairy tales were issued in three booklets by C. A. Reitzel in Copenhagen between May 1835 and April 1837. The first, of 8 May 1835, held "The Tinderbox", "Little Claus and Big Claus", "The Princess and the Pea" and "Little Ida's Flowers"; the first three were based on folktales he had heard in childhood. In June 1847 he visited England and met Charles Dickens. In 1857 he stayed five weeks at Dickens's home, Gads Hill Place, after which Dickens stopped writing to him, which Andersen never understood.

In early 1872 Andersen fell out of his bed and was severely hurt, and soon afterwards he showed signs of liver cancer. He died on 4 August 1875 at Rolighed, a country house near Copenhagen belonging to his friends Moritz G. Melchior and his wife. By then he was internationally revered, and the Danish government paid him an annual stipend as a national treasure. His 156 fairy tales in nine volumes have been translated into more than 125 languages and have inspired ballets, plays and films.
hans-holbein-the-younger: Holbein was born in the free imperial city of Augsburg, a son of the painter Hans Holbein the Elder, whose trade he and his older brother Ambrosius followed. By 1515 the brothers had moved to Basel, a centre of learning and the printing trade, where they were apprenticed to Hans Herbster and found work designing woodcuts and metalcuts for printers. That year they added pen drawings to the margins of a copy of Erasmus's The Praise of Folly, early evidence of Holbein's wit and humanist leaning.

Holbein travelled to England in 1526 with a recommendation from Erasmus and was welcomed into the circle of Sir Thomas More, who called him a wonderful artist. He painted the Portrait of Sir Thomas More and a group portrait of More's family, now known only from a sketch and copies. In Basel, where Luther's major works were first published, his Dance of Death of 1523 to 1526 refashioned the medieval danse macabre as a reformist satire in woodcuts.

Back in England in 1532, he found favour with the Boleyn family and Thomas Cromwell rather than with More's circle, and he portrayed Lutheran merchants of the Hanseatic League at the Steelyard. By 1535 he was King's Painter to Henry VIII, producing portraits, festive decorations and designs for jewellery, plate and other objects. Cromwell's execution in 1540 damaged his career. He kept his post, turned again to private commissions and painted some of his finest miniatures.

Holbein held that everything began with a drawing. He always made preparatory studies of his sitters, in black and coloured chalks on unprimed paper in his first English period and on pink-primed paper with pen and brush from 1532. His portraits were prized for their likeness, yet he embedded layers of symbolism and allusion in them. He added Italian elements, notably single-point perspective and antique motifs, to a style rooted in the late Gothic. About twelve certain miniatures survive, and many designs on Greenwich armour were based on his patterns.

Holbein died between 7 October and 29 November 1543. He founded no school, and his images of Henry VIII, Erasmus, More and Cromwell have fixed their appearance for posterity, leading John North to call him the cameraman of Tudor history. His friend Amerbach and Amerbach's son Basilius collected his work, forming the core of the Holbein collection at the Kunstmuseum Basel.
hanseatic-league: The Hansa grew from Lübeck and a few other North German towns in the late 12th century and expanded between the 13th and 15th centuries until it encompassed nearly 200 settlements across eight modern countries, from Estonia and Russia in the north-east to the Netherlands in the west. The Scandinavians had led Baltic trade before it, and the sailors of Gotland sailed up rivers as far as Novgorod. Well before the term Hanse appeared in a document in 1267, guilds, or hansas, formed in different cities to trade overseas, especially with the less developed eastern Baltic, which supplied timber, wax, amber, resins and furs. The dominant language of trade was Middle Low German.

The league established Kontors, trading posts with considerable legal autonomy, in Bruges, Bergen and London beside the Peterhof in Novgorod. The one in London, the Steelyard, grew into a walled community with warehouses, a weigh house, a church, offices and homes. The weakening of imperial power under the late Hohenstaufen dynasty pushed the towns to form a looser network of cities. The Hansa dominated maritime trade in the North and Baltic Seas, and its economic power enabled it to impose blockades and even wage war against kingdoms and principalities.

The league declined as transatlantic trade developed after the discovery of the Americas, and short-term contracts made its model of privileged guaranteed trade obsolete. Local feudal lords asserted control over towns, and Kiel was expelled in 1518 for harbouring pirates. By the mid-16th century its weak connections left it vulnerable, and it disintegrated in 1669.

Even at its peak the Hansa was a loosely aligned confederation with no permanent administrative body, treasury or standing military force, and it never became a legal person. Its one central institution was the Hansetag, an irregular diet that met in Lübeck; many towns did not attend, and decisions did not bind a city whose delegates were absent. The Grand Master of the Teutonic Order, the only autonomous landed state that was a member, was often seen as its head. Only a few members were free imperial cities, though many temporarily escaped domination by local nobility. Its most emblematic ship was the cog.
hanukkah: After the death of Alexander the Great in 323 BCE, Judea became part of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt. In 200 BCE King Antiochus III the Great of Syria defeated Ptolemy V Epiphanes at the Battle of Panium, and Judea passed to the Seleucid Empire. Antiochus III guaranteed the Jews their ancestral customs and the practice of their religion in the Temple. His son Antiochus IV Epiphanes reversed this policy, apparently after a dispute over the leadership of the Temple and the office of High Priest.

Some modern scholars, following the Second Book of Maccabees, see the king as intervening in a civil war between traditionalist Jews and a Hellenizing faction. These groups contested the office of High Priest, with figures bearing Hebrew or Aramaic names such as Onias set against Hellenizing priests with Greek names such as Jason and Menelaus.

In the traditional account, the Second Temple was looted and its services stopped, and Judaism was outlawed. In 167 BCE Antiochus IV ordered an altar to Zeus set up in the Temple, banned circumcision and had pigs sacrificed on the altar. The priest Mattathias and his five sons launched a revolt. After Mattathias died, his son Judah, known as Judas Maccabeus, took command and won campaigns against Seleucid forces.

In 164 BCE the rebels recovered Jerusalem and the Second Temple, which was cleansed and rededicated. The Jewish historian Josephus, in his Jewish Antiquities, says that Judas ordered yearly eight-day festivities, which Josephus calls the festival of Lights. The story is told in the First and Second Books of Maccabees, held canonical by the Roman Catholic and Orthodox Churches but not part of the Masoretic Text.

Hanukkah begins on 25 Kislev and lasts eight nights. Each night a light is added to the nine-branched menorah, the extra light, the shamash, being used to kindle the others. Customs include the hymn Ma'oz Tzur, the game of dreidel, gifts of money called gelt, and fried foods such as latkes and jam-filled doughnuts, recalling the tradition of a small flask of oil that kept the Temple's menorah alight for eight days.

The festival is of rabbinic origin and, in religious terms, relatively minor. It grew in cultural weight under Zionism, which stressed the Hasmonean victory, and in North America, where from the nineteenth century Reform leaders such as Isaac Mayer Wise made it a children's celebration. Because it often falls near Christmas, it also took on a role as a Jewish counterpart to the season's festivities.
harald-hardrada: Harald was born in Ringerike in Norway, in 1015 or possibly 1016, to Åsta Gudbrandsdatter and her second husband Sigurd Syr, a petty king of Ringerike and one of the strongest and wealthiest chieftains of the Uplands. Through his mother he was the youngest of three half-brothers of King Olaf Haraldsson, later Saint Olaf. In 1030, aged fifteen, he fought beside Olaf at the Battle of Stiklestad, where they were defeated by forces loyal to Cnut. Harald escaped to a remote farm, crossed into Sweden and reached Kievan Rus' about a year after the battle.

Grand Prince Yaroslav the Wise welcomed him and made him a captain of his forces. Around 1033 or 1034 Harald and about 500 men went on to Constantinople and joined the Varangian Guard. He was found fighting on nearly every frontier of the empire, against Arab pirates in the Mediterranean, in Asia Minor and probably against the Pechenegs, and Snorri Sturluson calls him leader over all the Varangians. He grew extremely rich and sent his wealth to Yaroslav for safekeeping.

Harald left Novgorod in early 1045 and reached Sigtuna in Sweden at the end of 1045 or early in 1046. In 1046 he joined Sweyn of Denmark in raids on the Danish coast, and Magnus the Good, unwilling to fight his uncle, agreed to share the kingship, which Harald held alone from the following year. He married Tora Torbergsdatter of a powerful Norwegian family to secure domestic support. Harald developed a Norwegian currency and a coin economy, started trade with Kievan Rus', the Byzantine Empire, Scotland and Ireland, and according to later sagas founded Oslo.

From 1048 until 1064 he raided Denmark almost every year in a war against Sweyn. In 1049 he pillaged and burned Hedeby, the most important Danish trade centre, which never recovered as a civil town. Although he won most engagements, he never occupied Denmark. His epithet harðráði has been translated as hard in counsel, tyrannical, ruthless, severe or resolute, and it is not clear it was used in his lifetime.

Tostig Godwinson invited Harald to claim the English throne, and in September 1066 Harald invaded northern England with 10,000 troops and 300 longships. He beat the forces of Northumbria and Mercia at the Battle of Fulford on 20 September, and York surrendered on 24 September. On 25 September Harold Godwinson's army surprised the Norwegians at Stamford Bridge, where Harald had brought only light armour, and Harald was killed early in the battle, struck in the throat by an arrow. His army was wiped out. His body was moved to Nidaros the next year. Historians often consider his death the end of the Viking Age.
harappa: Harappa lies in Punjab, about 24 kilometres west of Sahiwal, and takes its name from a modern village near the former course of the Ravi River. The river now runs eight kilometres to the north. Harappa and Mohenjo-daro were the two major cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation. Harappa is regarded as the type site of the civilisation, which is why it is sometimes called the Harappan civilisation, a term the Archaeological Survey of India has used more commonly since 1947.

The excavators divide the occupation into phases. The Ravi phase began around 3300 BCE, and the Kot Diji phase, c. 2800 to 2600 BCE, saw the settlement enclosed with massive mud-brick walls and platforms, with broad north-south streets and separate areas for housing and craft work. Trade was older than the city itself. Unfinished shell bangles show that raw shell was carried inland from the coast, and copper tools and beads of lapis lazuli, carnelian, agate and amazonite show links with sources in Gujarat, Rajasthan, Baluchistan and Afghanistan. In the Harappan phase, c. 2600 to 1900 BCE, the site covered at least 150 hectares.

From about 1900 BCE the civilisation slowly declined, and the Late Harappan phase lasted until about 1300 BCE. Seals, weights and writing went out of use, though faience making and some pottery techniques continued. Mortimer Wheeler once suggested that invaders had destroyed the cities, but later excavations at Harappa found no evidence of an invasion or destruction. The evidence points rather to natural causes, such as a gradual drying of the climate. Harappa itself may never have been completely abandoned.

Charles Masson was the first European to report on the ruins, in 1826. The mounds were still in good condition when Alexander Cunningham visited in 1853 and 1856, but they were then quarried for brick when the railway through Punjab was built. Cunningham estimated that they had supplied ballast for about 100 miles of the Lahore to Multan line.

Daya Ram Sahni began the first large-scale excavation in January 1921, and Wheeler dug in 1946. The Harappa Project of the University of California, Berkeley worked with Pakistan's Department of Archaeology from 1986, and fieldwork continued until 2010. In 2004 the site was added to the tentative list for UNESCO World Heritage Sites, and the modern town is a small crossroads town of about 15,000 people.
harar: Harar stands on a hilltop in the eastern part of Ethiopia, about 500 kilometres from Addis Ababa and 1,885 metres above sea level. Its people called it Harar-Gey, or simply Gey, meaning the city. For centuries it was a major commercial centre linked by trade routes with the rest of Ethiopia, the Horn of Africa, the Arabian Peninsula and Asia. The old walled city, Harar Jugol, covers about 60 hectares and is divided into five quarters. It has five ancient gates: Assum Bari, Argobba Bari, Suqutat Bari, Badro Bari and Asmadin Bari.

It is unclear when Harar was founded, and proposed dates run from a Qurayshi settlement in the late 7th century to a local creation in the 10th century. Islam had gained a foothold on the plateau by the 10th and 11th centuries through trade with Zeila, and by the 13th century it was the predominant religion. A history of the city records that the saint Abadir Umar ar-Rida and other religious leaders settled on the plateau about 1216.

In 1520 Harar became the capital of the Adal Sultanate under Sultan Abu Bakr ibn Muhammad. Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi, called Gragn, killed the sultan in 1525 and made Harar the centre of campaigns that ravaged most of Christian Ethiopia. After his defeat in 1543, his widow Bati del Wambara renewed the war, and in 1551 Nur ibn Mujahid married her and became ruler.

In the 17th century Ali ibn Da'ud founded the Emirate of Harar, a dynasty that ruled for the next two centuries. His successor Abdullah improved relations with the Oromo by marrying five of his sons to Oromo women, and the emirate extended its economic influence from Shewa to Zeila and began to mint its own coins. In 1887 the army of Menelik II conquered Harar and appointed his nephew Ras Makonnen as governor. Makonnen had the main mosque torn down and replaced it with an Orthodox church.

Harar is the capital of the Harari Region, and Harar Jugol was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2006. UNESCO describes it as considered the fourth holiest city of Islam, with 82 mosques, three of which date from the 10th century, and 102 shrines. Harari houses, called gey gar, form a distinct type whose layout dates back to 1754. They stand in walled compounds arranged around a courtyard. The French poet Arthur Rimbaud settled in Harar as a merchant between 1880 and 1891, and his house is one of its landmarks.
harare: Harare lies in north-eastern Zimbabwe, in the Mashonaland region, on one of the higher parts of the Highveld plateau at an elevation of 1,483 metres. Its climate is subtropical highland, cooler and drier than a tropical or subtropical climate because of the altitude and a cool south-easterly airflow. The original landscape could be described as parkland, and Harare Kopje, at 1,540 metres, is the highest point in the city. The name comes from the village near Harare Kopje of the Shona chief Neharawa, whose nickname was he who does not sleep.

The Pioneer Column, a military volunteer force of settlers organised by Cecil Rhodes for the British South Africa Company, founded the city as a fort on 12 September 1890. It was named Fort Salisbury after the British prime minister, the 3rd Marquess of Salisbury, and became known simply as Salisbury. Company administrators demarcated the city and ran it until Southern Rhodesia achieved responsible government in 1923. Salisbury was declared a municipality in 1897 and became a city in 1935.

After the Second World War the city expanded rapidly with its designation as capital of the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland from 1953 to 1963, with significant immigration from Great Britain, Southern Africa and, to a lesser extent, Southern Europe. Suburbs such as Alexandra Park and Mount Pleasant sprawled outwards as motor vehicle ownership grew, while mostly black suburbs like Highfield suffered from overcrowding. The Federation was dissolved in 1963. Ian Smith's Rhodesian Front government declared Rhodesia independent of the United Kingdom on 11 November 1965 and kept Salisbury as the capital, and the country was internationally recognised as independent under the name Zimbabwe on 18 April 1980.

The city was renamed Harare on 18 April 1982, the second anniversary of independence. Before the change the black residential area now called Mbare was known as Harari. Investment in education and healthcare produced a growing middle class, and the Eastgate Centre and the New Reserve Bank Tower became landmarks of the period.

Harare is the capital and largest city of Zimbabwe, with 1,849,600 inhabitants in the 2022 census and an estimated 2,487,209 in its metropolitan province, which also includes Chitungwiza, Epworth and Ruwa. It is the country's financial, commercial and communications centre and a trading centre for tobacco, maize, cotton and citrus fruits. About 90 percent of its people are Shona-speaking. The University of Zimbabwe, founded in 1952, is in the city, and the National Gallery, the National Archives and the Harare Gardens stand in its central district. The city hosted the 1995 All-Africa Games and the 2003 Cricket World Cup.
harbin: Harbin lies in southern Heilongjiang on the south bank of the middle Songhua River, at the south-eastern edge of the Songnen Plain. The terrain is generally flat and low. It is the northernmost of China's major cities and has long, dry and freezing winters, which have earned it the nickname Ice City. The city government says the name means 'swan' in Jurchen, while other sources derive it from a Manchu word meaning 'a place for drying fishing nets'.

Human settlement in the area dates from at least 2200 BCE. Wanyan Aguda, founder of the Jin dynasty, who reigned from 1115 to 1123, came from the Jurchen Wanyan tribes living near the Ashi River. In 1115 he established the Jin capital, Shangjing Huiningfu, in what is now Acheng District of Harbin. Wanyan Liang moved the capital to Yanjing, now Beijing, in 1153, and Wanyan Yong restored the city as a secondary capital in 1173.

The modern city dates from 1898, when the Russian Empire built the Chinese Eastern Railway. The Polish engineer Adam Szydłowski drew plans for the city, and the Russians made it the base of their administration of the railway. The settlement grew into a city within five years, with settlers from across the Russian Empire, including Ukrainians, Poles, Jews, Georgians and Tatars. In the 1920s it was considered China's fashion capital.

Japan invaded Manchuria after the Mukden Incident of September 1931, and Japanese forces occupied Harbin within hours. From 1932 until 1945 it was the largest city of the puppet state of Manchukuo. The Soviet Army took the city on 20 August 1945 and handed it to the People's Liberation Army in April 1946. Most of the European community left in the early 1950s, so that by 1964 the Russian population was reduced to 450.

Harbin is the capital and largest city of Heilongjiang, with a metropolitan population of 10,009,854 at the 2020 census. Its Russian and European legacy survives in Central Street and in Saint Sophia Cathedral. UNESCO named Harbin a City of Music in 2010, and the city is known for its winter ice sculpture festival.
hargeisa: Hargeisa lies in a valley in the Galgodon, or Ogo, highlands at an elevation of 1,334 metres. The Laas Geel complex on its outskirts holds Neolithic cave paintings in an excellent state of preservation, in ten rock alcoves. They show human figures with raised hands facing long-horned, humpless cattle, and a French team found them in 2002, though local people had known of them for centuries. The climate is hot and semi-arid but tempered by the altitude, with most of the roughly 400 millimetres of annual rain falling between April and September.

Oral poetic accounts say Hargeisa began as a watering and trading stop for nomads and caravans, and the modern settlement grew from the Big Commune founded around 1860 by Sheikh Madar Shirwa, a Qadiriyya scholar born in Berbera who had studied at Harar. He and his companions founded a religious commune, introducing farming on large sorghum plantations in place of pastoral wandering, caring for the sick and elderly and promoting a common religious identity above tribe. One account derives the name from Harar as-sagir, little Harar, another from a Somali phrase for a place to sell hides and skins.

In 1888 the British established a protectorate in British Somaliland with Berbera as its capital. The capital was later moved to Hargeisa, which was granted capital status in 1941. The protectorate became independent on 26 June 1960 and united days later with the former Italian Somaliland to form the Somali Republic. On 31 May 1988 the Somali National Movement attacked Hargeisa, and the government of Siad Barre answered with shelling and aerial bombardment of the city. Up to 90 percent of it was destroyed in what is described as the Isaaq genocide. After the collapse of the central government and the declaration of independence of the Republic of Somaliland, reconstruction began, financed largely by local entrepreneurs and by remittances from relatives abroad.

Hargeisa is the capital and largest city of Somaliland, a partially recognised state that is still considered internationally part of Somalia. It hosts the parliament, the presidential palace and the government ministries. Its population was estimated at about 30,000 in 1958. It is a commercial centre for retail, trading, construction and stone-cutting, and the University of Hargeisa is one of several colleges and universities there.
harju-county: Harju County lies on the southern coast of the Gulf of Finland and borders Lääne-Viru, Järva, Rapla and Lääne counties. The county has several islands, the largest of which is Naissaar, and Lahemaa National Park, created in 1971, was the first national park in the Soviet Union.

The modern county was formed from two ancient Estonian counties, Revala, around what is now Tallinn, and Harjumaa, which lay south of Revala. They were merged into one in 1266. Lindanise, a small trading post on the Gulf of Finland, was the capital of Revala and grew into the Hanseatic town of Reval and later Tallinn.

In 1219 King Valdemar II of Denmark landed at Lindanise and conquered Revala and Harju, and the inhabitants were forced into Christianity. During the Livonian Crusade the Order of the Sword Brothers took both counties, and they were given back to Denmark by the Treaty of Stensby in 1238.

The Danes built Toompea Castle in Tallinn, which in 1248 was the first settlement in Estonia to receive town rights, and in 1285 Tallinn became the northernmost member of the Hanseatic League. German dominance led to the St George's Night Uprising of 1343, which began with the burning of Padise Abbey, and Denmark then sold its possessions in northern Estonia to the Livonian Order. In 1561 the nobility of North Estonia and the Tallinn Town Council declared loyalty to Sweden.

During the Great Northern War the plague of 1710 to 1713 killed more than eighty percent of the county's population, and Russian forces took Tallinn in 1710 after a month's siege. Russian rule was secured by the Treaty of Nystad in 1721. The railway between Paldiski, Tallinn and Saint Petersburg opened in 1870.

The Republic of Estonia was proclaimed in Tallinn on 24 February 1918. The Soviet Union annexed Estonia on 6 August 1940, and a German occupation followed from 1941 to 1944, during which concentration camps were set up in northern Estonia. After the Soviet reoccupation Paldiski became a nuclear submarine training centre in 1962, a closed town until 1994. Harju County was replaced by raions in 1950 and re-formed in 1990, and Tallinn rejoined it in 1993.

Harju County is one of the fifteen counties of Estonia and contains the capital and largest city, Tallinn. It has 16 municipalities, and 614,567 people live there, which is almost half of the population of Estonia.
harold-godwinson: Harold was a son of Godwin, Earl of Wessex, and of Gytha Thorkelsdóttir, who was related to King Cnut. Around the time Edward the Confessor married Harold's sister Edith in January 1045, Harold became Earl of East Anglia. About then he began a relationship with Edith the Fair, a union in the Danish manner, more danico, which was not blessed by the Church but was accepted by most laypeople and counted as legitimate.

In 1051 the Godwins were driven into exile, but they raised an army that forced the king to restore them. Godwin died in 1053 and Harold succeeded him as Earl of Wessex, becoming the most powerful lay figure in England after the king.

In 1064 Harold was apparently shipwrecked at Ponthieu and taken to Duke William II of Normandy. Norman sources say he swore an oath on relics to support William's claim to the throne, and scholars disagree about the reliability of this story. In 1065 Harold supported Northumbrian rebels against his brother Tostig, who then allied with King Harald Hardrada of Norway.

Edward died on 5 January 1066, and the Witenagemot chose Harold the next day. He was crowned on 6 January, probably in Westminster Abbey. William began building about 700 ships and transports at Dives-sur-Mer.

Harold assembled troops on the Isle of Wight but disbanded them on 8 September when provisions ran out. Hardrada and Tostig landed the same day and defeated the earls Edwin and Morcar at Fulford on 20 September. Harold marched north from London, reached Yorkshire in four days and defeated them at Stamford Bridge on 25 September, where both were killed.

William's fleet set sail on 27 September and landed at Pevensey the next day. Harold marched about 390 kilometres south to meet him and set his army in earthworks near Hastings. On 14 October, after nine hours of fighting at Senlac Hill, Harold was killed and his brothers Gyrth and Leofwine with him. The sources for his death contradict each other.

A Norman poem says four knights lanced and dismembered him, twelfth-century histories say an arrow struck his head, and the Bayeux Tapestry shows a figure with an arrow in the eye, though that detail may be a later restoration. William of Poitiers says William gave the body to William Malet for burial by the sea. His sons Godwine and Edmund invaded England in 1068 and 1069 and were defeated at Northam in Devon.
harold-macmillan: Maurice Harold Macmillan was born on 10 February 1894 in Belgravia, London, the son of the publisher Maurice Crawford Macmillan and Helen Belles, an American from Spencer, Indiana. His grandfather Daniel MacMillan, who founded Macmillan Publishers, was the son of a Scottish crofter from the Isle of Arran. He was educated at Eton and Oxford. In the First World War he served in the Grenadier Guards and was wounded three times. At the Battle of Flers-Courcelette in September 1916 he lay for over twelve hours in a shell hole, reading Aeschylus in Greek, and he suffered pain and partial immobility for the rest of his life. He married Lady Dorothy Cavendish on 21 April 1920.

Macmillan won Stockton-on-Tees in 1924, lost it in 1929 and regained it in 1931 as a supporter of economic planning. He opposed the appeasement of Nazi Germany and first held office in 1940 at the Ministry of Supply. Late in 1942 he became British Minister Resident at Algiers. Under Churchill he became Minister of Housing in 1951, charged with building 300,000 houses a year, then Minister of Defence in 1954. Under Anthony Eden he was Foreign Secretary in 1955 and Chancellor of the Exchequer from December 1955.

When Eden resigned in 1957 after the Suez Crisis, Macmillan succeeded him as prime minister. In July 1957 he told the nation it had never had it so good, but warned of inflation, and he led the Conservatives to success in 1959 with an increased majority. He worked to rebuild the Special Relationship with the United States and presided over much of the decolonisation of Africa, beginning with the Gold Coast in 1957, citing the wind of change blowing across the continent. He ended National Service, acquired Polaris and pioneered the Nuclear Test Ban with the United States and the Soviet Union. A French veto blocked the United Kingdom's entry into the European Economic Community.

The Vassall affair, in which an Admiralty clerk was convicted in October 1962 of passing secrets to the Soviet Union, and the Profumo affair damaged his government. After a controversial Cabinet reshuffle he resigned the premiership in October 1963, citing ill health, and was succeeded by Lord Home. He stood down from the Commons at the 1964 election, after 37 years of service. He was Chancellor of the University of Oxford from 1960 until his death and chaired Macmillan Publishers from 1964 to 1974, publishing a multi-volume autobiography. He received the Order of Merit in 1976 and died on 29 December 1986, aged 92.
harran: Harran lies about 40 kilometres south-east of Urfa in south-eastern Turkey, at a crossroads between the Euphrates and the Tigris and on the border between the ancient Mesopotamian and Anatolian cultures. Its name goes back to the earliest documents that mention it, where it is written Ḫarrānu, meaning journey, caravan or crossroad. The Assyrians also called it Huzirina, the Greeks Kárrhai and the Romans Carrhae.

The earliest written records suggest that Harran was founded between about 2500 and 2000 BCE, possibly as a merchant outpost of traders from Ur. Tablets from Ebla of the 24th century BCE name a queen Zugalum as its ruler. Its place on trade routes made it a target for raids. Harran passed to Mitanni in the 16th century BCE and was conquered by the Assyrian king Adad-nirari I. It became a fortified provincial capital second only to Assur, and its temple of the moon god Sin, the Eḫulḫul, was consulted and renovated by many Mesopotamian rulers. Harran was the last capital of the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 612 to 609 BCE.

It then came under the Neo-Babylonian, Achaemenid, Macedonian and Seleucid empires, and many Greeks settled there. In 53 BCE the Battle of Carrhae, one of the worst defeats in Roman history, was fought there. The moon cult lasted long into the Middle Ages, and the city was sometimes called Hellenopolis, city of the pagan Greeks. In the winter of 639-640 the pagans of Harran negotiated its surrender to the Rashidun general Iyad ibn Ghanm, who gave them a new moon temple. Harran was briefly the capital of the Umayyad Caliphate from 744 to 750 and again of the Numayrid Emirate from 990 to 1081. The Mongols conquered it in 1260 and largely destroyed it in 1271.

Harran is a district of Şanlıurfa Province. Its old town is largely surrounded by ancient walls about 4.5 kilometres long, which once had 187 bastions. The Harran Castle is a large brick fortress of unknown date. The town is known for its beehive houses, which resemble domed buildings shown in Assyrian reliefs of the 7th century BCE.
harry-s-truman: Harry S. Truman was born in Lamar, Missouri, on 8 May 1884, the oldest child of John Anderson Truman and Martha Ellen Young Truman. His middle initial honours both his grandfathers and is not an abbreviation of one name. His father was a farmer and livestock dealer, and the family settled in Independence, Missouri, when Harry was six. He was refused an appointment to West Point because of poor eyesight and served in the Missouri National Guard from 1905 to 1911.

When the United States entered World War I on 6 April 1917, Truman rejoined his battery and fought in France as a captain in the Field Artillery. In 1919 he married Bess Wallace. He and Edward Jacobson opened a haberdashery in Kansas City, which went bankrupt in the recession of 1921.

Truman was elected a judge of Jackson County in 1922 and a senator for Missouri in 1934. From 1940 to 1944 he gained national prominence as chairman of the Truman Committee, which aimed to reduce waste and inefficiency in wartime contracts. He was nominated as Franklin D. Roosevelt's running mate, though reluctant, and was sworn in as vice president on 20 January 1945. He became president on Roosevelt's death in April. Only then was he told about the Manhattan Project and the atomic bomb.

As president Truman authorized the use of nuclear weapons against the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, set up the Marshall Plan and established the Truman Doctrine. He supported the founding of NATO and presided over the onset of the Cold War in 1947 and the Berlin Airlift in 1948. When Congress refused his proposal for comprehensive civil rights legislation, he issued orders that prohibited discrimination in federal agencies and desegregated the armed forces. He won the 1948 election against Thomas E. Dewey. The Korean War lasted from 1950 to 1953. Corruption in parts of his administration, which did not implicate Truman himself, became a campaign issue in 1952, and he chose not to run again.

In retirement Truman founded his presidential library and published his memoirs. He was admitted to hospital in Kansas City with pneumonia on 5 December 1972, developed multiple organ failure and died on 26 December, aged 88. When he left office in 1953 his administration was heavily criticised, but public feeling towards him grew warmer over the following decades.
harsha-of-kashmir: Harsha, also called Harshadeva, was born in 1059, the son of King Kalasha of Kashmir. Almost everything known of him comes from the Rajatarangini of Kalhana, whose father Champaka had been one of Harsha's ministers and who wrote in the time of Jayasimha, between 1127 and 1159. According to Kalhana he was built like a god and extremely handsome. He is said to have begun as a capable and noble king before his spending brought him into financial trouble.

Extravagant outlay on his troops and on pleasures left the king in grave difficulties. The historian Prithvi Nath Kaul Bamzai notes Kalhana's statement that even night soil was taxed. An accidental discovery of hoarded treasure at the Bhimasahi temple led him to despoil other temples and to melt down gold and silver images. Kalhana writes that not one temple kept its images, and that only two chief divine images were respected, Ranaswamin in the city and Martanda. Two colossal statues of the Buddha were saved by requests made one at Parihasapura by the singer Kanaka and one in the city by the monk Kusalsri.

Kalhana calls him that Turushka, and he bore the epithet raja-Turushka, Turk king. Turkish troops served him as mercenaries, and the chronicle says he continually supported Turushka captains-of-hundreds with money, while adding that he ate domesticated pigs until his death. According to the historian André Wink, Harsha in all likelihood took up the Muslim tradition of iconoclasm, as the epithet indicates. Kalhana also charges him with credulity towards parasites at court, who passed off slave girls as goddesses, and with incest with his sisters and violence against Naga, his father's sister's daughter.

Harsha died on 31 August 1101, the last ruler of the First Lohara dynasty. His conduct has remained a subject of discussion. The great Buddha of the capital outlived him: Kalhana records that when a fire reduced the city to a heap of earth in the reign of Sussala, the statue alone stood visible, blackened by smoke. The statue at Parihasapura had been made by Lalitaditya Muktapida, and Abul-Fazl states that the temples of that place were finally destroyed by Sikandar Butshikan, who ruled from 1389 to 1413.
hartford-connecticut: Hartford lies on the west bank of the Connecticut River, which forms the boundary between Hartford and East Hartford. The city covers about 47 square kilometres, of which about 1.8 square kilometres is water. It is bordered by the towns of West Hartford, Newington, Wethersfield, East Hartford, Bloomfield, South Windsor, Glastonbury and Windsor. Several Algonquian peoples lived in or around the area, including the Podunks east of the river, the Poquonocks, the Massacoes, the Tunxis, the Wangunks, and the Saukiog in Hartford itself.

The first Europeans known to have explored the area were the Dutch under Adriaen Block, who sailed up the Connecticut River in 1614. Dutch fur traders from New Amsterdam returned in 1623 to establish a trading post for the Dutch West India Company, partly to control the flow of wampum, the de facto currency of New Netherland and parts of New England. Their fort, Fort Hoop or the House of Hope, stood on the south bank of the Park River. In 1633 Jacob Van Curler formally bought the land around it from the Pequot chief. The fort was abandoned by 1654, and the area is still called Dutch Point.

Hartford alternated with New Haven as dual capital of Connecticut from 1664 and has been the sole capital since 1875. On 15 December 1814 delegates from the five New England states met at the Hartford Convention to discuss New England's possible secession from the United States. In the early nineteenth century the area was a centre of abolitionist activity, notably through the Beecher family: the minister Lyman Beecher, his daughter Harriet Beecher Stowe, author of Uncle Tom's Cabin, and Isabella Beecher Hooker, a leading figure in the women's rights movement. The American School for the Deaf, founded by Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet in 1817, was the first school for deaf children in the country.

After the American Civil War Hartford was the richest city in the United States for several decades. The Connecticut River reached a record flood stage in April 1909. On 6 July 1944 a fire at a performance of the Ringling Brothers and Barnum and Bailey Circus, known as the Hartford Circus Fire, killed 168 people, mostly children and their mothers.

Hartford is the capital of Connecticut and the core of the Greater Hartford metropolitan area, which has about 1.17 million residents. The city itself had a population of 121,054 at the 2020 census. It is nicknamed the Insurance Capital of the World, and the industry remains the region's largest. The city holds the Wadsworth Atheneum, the oldest continuously operating public art museum in the country, Bushnell Park, and the Mark Twain House, where Mark Twain wrote his best-known works. The Hartford Courant, founded in 1764, is the oldest continuously published newspaper in the United States.
harun-al-rashid: Harun was born in Rey, the son of the third Abbasid caliph, al-Mahdi, and his wife al-Khayzuran, a woman of strong character who greatly influenced affairs of state under her husband and sons. His birth date is debated, with sources giving dates from 763 to 766. He devoted most of his time to hadith and the Quran and trained in swordplay and archery. In 780 and again in 782 he nominally led campaigns against the Byzantine Empire under Empress Irene; the second reached the Asian suburbs of Constantinople. His raids raised his standing and earned him the title al-Rashid, the Rightly-Guided One. He was made crown prince and given the western territories from Syria to Azerbaijan.

Harun became caliph in September 786, in his early twenties, when his brother al-Hadi died. On his accession he led Friday prayers in Baghdad's Great Mosque. His mother kept a strong hand in government until her death in 789. His vizier Yahya ibn Khalid and Yahya's sons, especially Ja'far, of the Iranian family of the Barmakids, generally controlled the administration, and the position of Persians at court peaked in his reign. Their fall is more likely due to behaviour Harun found disrespectful, such as entering his court unannounced and deciding matters of state without consulting him; al-Fadl ibn al-Rabi succeeded Yahya as chief minister. In 796 he moved his court and government to Raqqa.

Envoys travelled between his court and that of Charlemagne, king of the Franks, discussing Christian access to holy sites and exchanging gifts. In 802 Harun sent silks, ivory chessmen, a large tent, an elephant named Abul-Abbas and a water clock whose mechanical knights emerged one for each hour. Both rulers had common interests: Charlemagne's conflict with Cordoba and the Byzantine opposition to his claim to the imperial title. In 805 Harun defeated Emperor Nikephoros I at the Battle of Krasos, and in 807 his forces occupied Cyprus.

A major revolt led by Rafi ibn al-Layth in Samarqand drew Harun east to Khorasan in 808. He became ill and died in March 809 at Sanabad in Tus, and was buried in the summer palace of the governor, Humayd ibn Qahtaba. His son al-Amin succeeded him. The place later became known as Mashhad. Anecdotes gathered round him for centuries, and Saadi of Shiraz put several into his Gulistan, while parts of One Thousand and One Nights are set in his court. Al-Masudi wrote that the splendour and riches of his reign were such that the period was called the Honeymoon.
harvard-university: Harvard was founded and authorised by the Great and General Court of the Massachusetts Bay Colony. Its first headmaster, Nathaniel Eaton, took office the following year, and in 1638 the college acquired English North America's first known printing press. In the same year John Harvard, a Puritan clergyman who had emigrated from England, bequeathed it £780 and his library of some 320 volumes, and the college was named in his honour. Its earliest known official seal, of 1650, bears the motto In Christi Gloriam, To the glory of Christ. Although never formally affiliated with any Protestant denomination, Harvard trained Congregational clergy until its curriculum and student body were gradually secularised in the 18th century.

Harvard faculty and students largely supported the Patriot cause in the American Revolution. The Constitution of Massachusetts recognised the college as a university in 1780. In the 19th century Enlightenment ideas of reason and free will, widespread among Congregational ministers, set liberals against more traditional Calvinist pastors. The election of Henry Ware as Hollis professor of divinity in 1805 and the appointment of the liberal Samuel Webber as president in 1807 marked a shift to more liberal and Arminian ideas.

Under President Charles William Eliot, who served from 1869 to 1909, Harvard developed several professional schools and became a modern research university. Eliot, a chemist who had studied two years in Germany, used the German model: a graduate department formed in 1872 granted its first PhD degrees in 1873. Harvard Law School was established in 1817 through a bequest of 1779 by Isaac Royall Jr., and Harvard Business School in 1908. In 1900 Harvard became a founding member of the Association of American Universities, and James B. Conant led it through the Great Depression and the Second World War.

Harvard Yard in Cambridge, Massachusetts, holds Massachusetts Hall, built between 1718 and 1720 and the oldest building still standing. The university has three campuses, in Cambridge, in Allston and in Boston's Longwood Medical Area. Harvard Library, centred on Widener Library, holds more than 20 million volumes. The Harvard Crimson student newspaper, founded in 1873, counts among its alumni the presidents Franklin D. Roosevelt and John F. Kennedy.
haryana: Haryana is a landlocked state in north-western India. It is bordered by Punjab and Himachal Pradesh to the north, Rajasthan to the west and south and Delhi to the south-east, while the Yamuna forms its eastern boundary with Uttar Pradesh. Most of it lies on the fertile Ghaggar Plain, part of the Indo-Gangetic Plain, and its highest point is Karoh Peak, 1,467 metres, in the Sivalik Hills. Some anthropologists believe the name comes from the period after the Mahabharata, when the Abhiras are thought to have settled there and developed advanced agricultural techniques.

The villages of Rakhigarhi in Hisar district and Bhirrana in Fatehabad district hold ancient sites of the Indus Valley Civilisation, with evidence of paved roads, drainage, terracotta brick and skilled metalworking. In the seventh century the Pushyabhuti dynasty ruled parts of northern India from Thanesar, and Harsha was its prominent king. The Tomara dynasty ruled the south of the region in the tenth century. In the British period the area was part of the province of Punjab, with princely states such as Jind, Kalsia, Loharu and Pataudi.

At the Partition of India, Punjab was divided between India and Pakistan, and Haryana became part of East Punjab. A significant number of Muslims left for Pakistan, and a huge number of Hindu and Sikh refugees arrived from West Punjab. The modern state was formed on 1 November 1966 under the Punjab Reorganisation Act. The Shah Commission, set up in April 1966, fixed the boundaries by the languages people spoke. Haryana took the predominantly Hindi-speaking south of the former Punjab, while Punjab kept the area where Punjabi speakers formed the majority.

The capital is Chandigarh, shared with Punjab. Gurgaon is among India's large financial and technology centres, and Faridabad is the most populous city. The state surrounds Delhi on three sides, so a large part of it lies within the National Capital Region. Hindi is the official language, and Punjabi has been a second official language since 2010. The 2011 census counted 25,351,462 people.
hasan-ibn-ali: Hasan ibn Ali was born in Medina in about 625, the firstborn of Muhammad's daughter Fatima and Muhammad's cousin Ali. Hasan was raised in Muhammad's household until the prophet's death, when he was about seven, and early sources widely report Muhammad's love for him and his brother Husayn. He is part of the ahl al-bayt, Muhammad's family, and of the ahl al-kisa, which comprises Muhammad, Ali, Fatima and their two sons.

Hasan did not play a major role under the first three caliphs, Abu Bakr, Umar and Uthman. After Ali became caliph he were sent to Kufa, where they raised an army of some 6,000 men, and Hasan fought in the Battle of the Camel in 656 against Aisha, Talha and Zubayr.

After Ali was assassinated by the Kharijite Abd al-Rahman ibn Muljam in January 661, Hasan was acknowledged caliph in Kufa. Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, the governor of Syria, did not recognise him and marched an army of sixty thousand men to Maskin, north of present-day Baghdad, while urging Hasan in letters to give up his claim.

Hasan sent a vanguard under Ubayd Allah ibn al-Abbas, but he was severely wounded in an attempted assassination by a Kharijite, which demoralised his army and led to widespread desertion. Ubayd Allah and most of his troops also defected after Mu'awiya bribed him. In August 661 Hasan signed a peace treaty with Mu'awiya on the condition that Mu'awiya should rule in accordance with the Quran and the Sunnah, that a council should name his successor and that Hasan's supporters should receive an amnesty. He ruled as caliph from January until August 661, then withdrew to Medina and did not engage in politics.

Hasan most likely died on 2 April 670. The early sources are nearly unanimous that he was poisoned, and Mu'awiya is usually identified as the instigator. His death removed an obstacle to the succession of Mu'awiya's son Yazid I.

Critics have called the treaty with Mu'awiya a sign of weakness. His supporters hold that abdication was inevitable after his soldiers mutinied and that he sought unity and peace among Muslims, which a Sunni hadith says Muhammad had foretold. In Shia Islam Hasan is the second Imam, who succeeded Ali and was followed by his brother Husayn, and the imamate and the caliphate are viewed as separate institutions.
hasidism: In the late 17th century several trends came together among the Jews of the southern edge of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, especially in what is now Western Ukraine. The most prominent was the spread of Kabbalah, once an esoteric teaching practised by a few, through cheap printed pamphlets. The same current had fed the Sabbatean movement of Sabbatai Zevi, who declared himself Messiah in 1665. Israel ben Eliezer, about 1698 to 1760, called the Baal Shem Tov, is regarded as the founder. He was a folk healer who became wealthy and well known, and most of what is told of him comes from hagiographic accounts. His follower Dov Ber, the Maggid of Mezhirichi, succeeded him and turned his ideas into a movement.

Hasidic thought draws heavily on Lurianic Kabbalah and to an extent popularises it. Its most basic theme is the immanence of God in the universe. Its defining doctrine is that of the tzadik, the Righteous One, also called the Rebbe, as an inspiration and the figure around whom followers are organised. Hasidim are organised in independent groups called courts or dynasties, each headed by a hereditary Rebbe, and these often keep the name of the Eastern European town where they began, as Satmar, Belz and Vizhnitz do.

Worship stresses devotion, and wordless melodies called nigunim are a means of reaching devekut, cleaving to God, in prayer and communal gatherings. Many Hasidim use Galician Yiddish among themselves. Hasidic tales, a genre of hagiographies and anecdotes, were often passed on orally, and the earliest collection dates from 1815.

Early in the 19th century the tzaddiqim became a leading power across most of Eastern Europe, even in Lithuania, a stronghold of the opposing Misnagdic camp. Less than three generations after the Baal Shem Tov's death the movement had hundreds of thousands of followers by 1830. In the early 20th century emigration to America, urbanisation, World War I and the Russian Civil War uprooted the shtetls that had been its base. In the Soviet Union repression of religion brought rapid secularisation, though a few Hasidim, especially of Chabad, practised in secret for decades. Today most Hasidim live in Israel and the United States.
hasselt: Hasselt lies between the Campine region, north of the Demer, and the Hesbaye region to the south. The name derives from the Germanic word Hasaluth, which refers to the common hazel.

Hasselt was founded in about the 7th century on the Helbeek, a tributary of the Demer. In the Middle Ages it became one of the free cities of the county of Loon, whose borders were roughly those of the present province of Limburg. It is first named in a document in 1165. In 1232 Arnold IV, Count of Loon, gave the city the same freedoms as those enjoyed in Liège. From 1366 the county was ruled directly by the Prince-Bishopric of Liège, until annexation by France in 1794.

Under the First French Empire Maastricht was the capital of the Department of the Lower Meuse. After the defeat of Napoleon in 1815 the area became part of the United Kingdom of the Netherlands, and King William I renamed the department after the medieval Duchy of Limburg, a duchy that had never included Hasselt or Maastricht. Belgium split from the Netherlands in 1830, but the status of Limburg was settled only in 1839, when it was divided into Belgian and Dutch parts. Hasselt became the provisional capital of the Belgian province. In ecclesiastical terms Belgian Limburg became independent of the Diocese of Liège only in 1967, when Hasselt became the seat of a new diocese.

Hasselt is known for jenever, a gin. It escaped the ban on the production and sale of the drink imposed in 1601 by Albert VII, Archduke of Austria, and Isabella Clara Eugenia, because it belonged to the Prince-Bishopric of Liège. Jenever production was the most important industry in Limburg in the 19th century, with most distilleries in Hasselt.

Hasselt is the capital and largest city of the province of Limburg in the Flemish Region of Belgium and the seat of the Catholic diocese of Hasselt. The Gothic St Quentin's Cathedral, begun in the 11th century, and the Refuge of Herkenrode Abbey, of 1542, the city's oldest civic building, stand there, and Hasselt University was established in 1971.
hastings-banda: Hastings Kamuzu Banda was born Akim Kamnkhwala Mtunthama Banda near Kasungu, to Mphonongo Banda and Akupingamnyama Phiri. No birth was registered, so his date of birth is unknown. After attending village and mission schools he was baptised in 1910. He studied at the Wilberforce Institute in Ohio, graduating from its high school section in 1928, and later at the University of Edinburgh, which awarded him the Scottish Triple Qualification in 1941.

He became an elder of a parish in the Church of Scotland. In 1951 he moved to the Gold Coast, and Malawian Congress leaders, among them Henry Chipembere and Kanyama Chiume, later asked him to return and lead their cause.

Banda opposed the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland, formed in 1953, because he feared it would cost Nyasaland's Africans further rights. He reached Nyasaland on 6 July 1958 after an absence of about 42 years and toured the country speaking against the federation. By February 1959 Rhodesian troops had been flown in and a state of emergency declared. On 3 March he was arrested in Operation Sunrise and held in Gwelo in Southern Rhodesia.

He was released in April 1960 and invited to London for talks on independence. After elections in August 1961 he became de facto prime minister, a title formally granted on 1 February 1963. In December 1962 the British Secretary of State R. A. Butler essentially agreed to end the federation.

A month after independence Banda dismissed four ministers who had proposed limits on his powers, and the dissidents fled the country. The constitution of 6 July 1966 made Malawi a republic and Banda its first president, the only candidate, and formally made the Malawi Congress Party the sole legal party. The party made him president for life in 1970, and the legislature did the same for the country in 1971. His title included the word Ngwazi, meaning saviour or conqueror in Chichewa.

In 1983 three ministers and a member of parliament who had favoured multiparty politics died in what was officially a traffic accident. Adult citizens had to carry party cards, the Malawi Young Pioneers acted as the party's paramilitary wing, and films and books were censored. Human rights groups estimate that at least 6,000 people were killed, tortured or jailed without trial. With the end of the Cold War, donors pressed for reform, and in 1993 Banda agreed to a referendum that ended the one-party system. He was defeated in the elections that followed and died in South Africa on 25 November 1997.
hathor: Cattle imagery is frequent in the art of Predynastic Egypt, as are images of women with upraised, curved arms like horns, and both may represent goddesses connected with cattle. The Gerzeh Palette, from the Naqada II period, shows a cow's head with inward-curving horns surrounded by stars, which suggests a link with the sky.

Hathor herself is not unambiguously mentioned or depicted until the Fourth Dynasty, c. 2613 to 2494 BCE, although some objects that refer to her may be earlier. When she does clearly appear, her horns curve outward. Her Egyptian name, ḥwt-ḥr, is usually translated as house of Horus, but it can also mean my house is the sky.

The Egyptologist Robyn Gillam calls Hathor a type of deity rather than a single entity, and suggests that the royal goddess promoted by the Old Kingdom court absorbed many local goddesses, who were then treated as her manifestations. Texts speak of Seven Hathors, and sometimes of as many as 362.

As a sky goddess she was mother or consort of Horus and Ra, and so the symbolic mother of the pharaohs. She was also one of the goddesses who acted as the Eye of Ra. Her other concerns were music, dance, love, sexuality and motherhood, and the sistrum, a rattle, was important in her worship. The Seven Hathors appear in New Kingdom tales at births, foretelling how the characters will die.

She was shown as a cow, as a woman with a cow's head, and most often as a woman wearing a headdress of cow horns and a sun disk. Hathor also helped the dead cross into the Duat, and the Theban necropolis was portrayed as a mountain with her cow emerging from it.

From the Fourth Dynasty Hathor was the goddess most closely linked with the king, and late Old Kingdom rulers promoted her cult in the provinces to bind those regions to the court. More temples were dedicated to her than to any other Egyptian goddess. At Dendera, her oldest temple in Upper Egypt, which dates to at least the Fourth Dynasty, kings made additions across Egyptian history, and the last version, from the Ptolemaic and Roman periods, is among the best preserved of that time.

Many festivals involved drinking and dancing, such as the Festival of Drunkenness on the twentieth day of the month of Thout. In households women prayed to her for children, and the only known surviving birth brick is decorated with an image of a woman holding her child between images of Hathor. Isis increasingly overshadowed her after the New Kingdom, but she continued to be venerated until the early centuries CE.
hatshepsut: Hatshepsut was the eldest daughter of Thutmose I and his great royal wife Ahmose. After her father's death she was married to her half-brother Thutmose II, when she was fourteen or fifteen. The couple had at least one daughter, Princess Neferure. When Thutmose II died, his son Thutmose III inherited the throne as a child of two, and Hatshepsut ruled first as his regent.

By the seventh year of the reign of Thutmose III, around 1472 BCE, she had assumed the position of pharaoh beside him, taking the full royal titulary and sharing his regnal count, which backdated her accession to Year 1. Thutmose III became junior coregent. She is depicted in statues with the regalia of the office, including a false beard, and the images are seen as symbolic. Priests told a story of divine birth in which Amun conceived her through her mother, and the Oracle of Amun proclaimed her pharaoh.

She re-established trade networks disrupted during the Hyksos occupation and funded an expedition to the Land of Punt, around Year 9, which returned with 31 living myrrh trees and frankincense. She was one of the most prolific builders in Egypt. She erected twin obelisks at Karnak and built the Red Chapel and the Temple of Pakhet, which the Greeks called the Speos Artemidos. Her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari, with its focal point Djeser-Djeseru, is considered a masterpiece of ancient architecture. Her last dated attestation is Year 20, and she no longer appears in Year 22.

Her death is presumed in Year 22 of Thutmose III. She was probably buried in KV20 in the Valley of the Kings with her father, though Thutmose I was later moved to another tomb. A mummy from tomb KV60 was proposed in 2007 as hers, partly because a molar found in a canopic box seemed to fit its jaw, but in 2011 the tooth was identified as a lower molar while the mummy lacked an upper one, casting doubt on the identification.

Late in the reign of Thutmose III and into that of his son Amenhotep II, her cartouches and images were chiselled from walls and her statues at Deir el-Bahari were torn down and buried in a pit. Why this was done is not clear; scholars have proposed political necessity, the securing of Amenhotep II's uncertain claim, and a ritual deactivation of statues. The erasure confused nineteenth-century Egyptologists such as Jean-Francois Champollion, who found feminine verbs beside a bearded king. James Henry Breasted called her the first great woman in history of whom we are informed.
hattusa: The earliest traces of settlement on the site date from the 6th millennium BCE. Toward the end of the 3rd millennium BCE the Hattian people settled there and called the place Hattush. Assyrian merchants set up a trading post there in the 19th and 18th centuries BCE. A burned layer shows the city was destroyed around 1700 BCE; King Anitta of Kussara took credit and erected an inscribed curse on anyone who resettled it. The city was nevertheless rebuilt. Around 1650 BCE the Hittite king Labarna moved the capital from Neša to Hattusa and took the name Hattusili, the man from Hattusa.

The capital later moved north to Sapinuwa under Tudhaliya I after attacks by the Kaskians, and south to Tarhuntassa under Muwatalli II. In the mid-13th century BCE Mursili III returned the seat to Hattusa, where it remained until the end of the Hittite kingdom in the 12th century BCE.

At its peak the city covered 1.8 square kilometres, in an inner and an outer part surrounded by massive walls erected under Suppiluliuma I, c. 1344 to 1322 BCE. The inner city held a citadel with large administrative buildings and temples, and the royal residence stood on a high ridge called Büyükkale. The outer city to the south had elaborate gateways decorated with reliefs of warriors, lions and sphinxes, and four temples. Modern estimates put the population at around 10,000. Houses of timber and mud brick have vanished, leaving only the stone walls of temples and palaces.

The city was destroyed with the Hittite state around 1200 BCE, as part of the Late Bronze Age collapse. Excavations suggest it was abandoned gradually over several decades, and a regional drought has been suggested. The final burning probably came after the royal family, elites and state apparatus had left, and agricultural communities with a different material culture settled in the ruins as early as the 12th century BCE.

The French archaeologist Charles Texier brought attention to the ruins after his visit in 1834. In 1905 and 1906 Hugo Winckler of the German Oriental Society began excavating the royal fortress. Thousands of tablets were recovered, mostly in the then unreadable Hittite language, and a few Akkadian texts identified the site as Hattusa. Systematic German excavations continue, and the site was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1986.

About 30,000 clay tablets from Hattusa form the main corpus of Hittite literature, among them official correspondence, contracts, legal codes, cult procedures and oracles. One tablet records the terms of a peace between the Hittites and Egypt under Ramesses II after the Battle of Kadesh, in 1259 or 1258 BCE.
haute-savoie: Haute-Savoie takes its name from the historical region of Savoy, as does the neighbouring department of Savoie to the south. To the north it borders the Swiss canton of Geneva and Lake Geneva, to the east the canton of Valais and Italy's Aosta Valley, and to the west the department of Ain. It has the largest range of elevations of any French department: its lowest point is 250 m in the Rhône Valley and its highest is Mont Blanc, at 4,810 m. Because the country is mountainous, passes matter to trade and economic life, among them the Col de la Forclaz and the Mont Blanc Tunnel, which links Chamonix to Courmayeur.

Savoy was governed by the House of Savoy from 1032 to 1860, and the Dukes of Savoy ruled the region from 1416 to 1720. After the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713 the territory of modern Haute-Savoie and neighbouring Savoie became part of the Kingdom of Sardinia. France annexed the region by the Treaty of Turin, formalised on 24 March 1860.

From November 1942 to September 1943 Haute-Savoie was under military occupation by Fascist Italy. The Maquis des Glières, a band of Free French Resistance fighters, operated from the department. In the winter of 1943–1944 German troops burned down around 500 farms in response to Resistance activity. The first Winter Olympic Games were held at Chamonix in 1924.
havana: Havana lies on the northern coast of Cuba along the Straits of Florida, south of the Florida Keys, where the Gulf of Mexico joins the Atlantic Ocean. The city extends mostly westward and southward from a bay, which is entered through a narrow inlet and divides into three main harbours. The Almendares River crosses the city from south to north.

The city stands mostly on low hills. A limestone ridge about 60 metres high slopes up from the east and culminates in the heights of La Cabaña and El Morro, where the Spanish built fortifications overlooking the eastern bay.

In the early 16th century Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar founded the town of San Cristóbal de la Habana on the southern coast of Cuba, at the mouth of the Mayabeque River, now the town of Batabanó.
